subject: Chlorpromazine
context: Chlorpromazine, a phenothiazine carrying an amine side chain on its 10-nitrogen, was the only compound among those tested that failed to protect HT-22 cells in the rotenone neurotoxicity model. The 10-N substitution causes a roughly 1000-fold loss of potency relative to methylene blue in glutamate, IAA, and rotenone assays, and abolishes the complex I-to-cytochrome c electron shunt, oxygen consumption enhancement, and glycolysis suppression. In the lysate oxidation assay chlorpromazine increased DCF fluorescence with or without mitochondria and NADH, behaving as a pro-oxidant and explaining its weak neuroprotection.
source_document: _document_ - Neuroprotective Actions of Methylene Blue and Its Derivatives.md

subject: Creatine
context: Sarcopenia is an age-related condition marked by declining muscle mass, strength, and functional capacity. Creatine supplementation combined with resistance training is an effective countermeasure: studies in older adults (>65 years) taking 5 g/day during heavy resistance training promoted greater gains in muscle mass and isometric strength, and meta-analyses confirm that older individuals doing resistance training gain more muscle mass, strength, and functional capacity when supplementing creatine. Creatine also preserves muscle mass and promotes fat loss during energy-restricted diets, helping manage adult-onset obesity while preventing the muscle loss that commonly accompanies weight loss in older individuals.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine supplementation has been reported to lower plasma homocysteine, an effect that may reduce cardiovascular disease risk. Because homocysteine is methylated back to methionine by enzymes that require the same methyl-donor pool (S-adenosyl methionine) used for creatine synthesis, supplying exogenous creatine spares methyl groups that would otherwise be consumed in endogenous creatine formation, thereby lowering homocysteine production. Studies in individuals adhering to vegan diets (who tend to have elevated homocysteine) reported that creatine supplementation reduced homocysteine levels and improved systemic microvascular endothelial function, supporting creatine's role in cardiovascular health beyond its direct effects on muscle bioenergetics.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine down-regulates the expression of toll-like receptors, including TLR-2, TLR-3, TLR-4, and TLR-7, in a mouse macrophage cell line (RAW 254.7). This downregulation could reduce the ability to sense some infections in immunocompromised individuals, but TLR-4 downregulation may also alter Parkinson's disease pathology and inhibit neuronal death as the disease progresses. Creatine's influence on toll-like receptors is one component of its broader immunomodulatory effects, which also include altering cytokine production, possibly through the NF-kB signaling pathway, thereby affecting cytokines, receptors, and growth factors that shape immune responses and inflammation.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine supplementation increases brain phosphocreatine content by 5-15% and enhances brain bioenergetics, which is thought to underlie its cognitive benefits. Studies report that creatine attenuates mental fatigue and improves cognition, executive function, working memory, and processing speed, especially in older adults and during sleep deprivation. Examples include improved working memory and processing speed after 5 g/day for 6 weeks, better maintenance of mood, balance, and reaction time after sleep deprivation, and improved long-term memory and random number generation in elderly participants. While not all studies show benefit, the evidence supports creatine as a modest cognitive enhancer, particularly under metabolic or cognitive stress.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine supplementation is one of the most studied and effective ergogenic aids for athletes. It increases muscle creatine and phosphocreatine levels, enhances acute exercise capacity, and improves training adaptations, yielding roughly 10-20% improvements in high-intensity exercise tasks across fitness activities, golf, volleyball, soccer, softball, ice hockey, running, and swimming. The International Society of Sports Nutrition concludes creatine is the most effective ergogenic supplement available for increasing high-intensity exercise capacity and lean body mass during training. Ergogenic benefits are seen in men and women across ages from children to the elderly, although most studies have been conducted in men.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine augments the anticancer efficacy of the metabolite methylglyoxal (MG). Creatine content and energy availability are low in several types of malignant cells and in the T cells that mediate immune responses against cancer, and the creatine transporter SLC6A8 is markedly increased in tumor-infiltrating immune cells. Patra et al. reported that MG efficacy is significantly augmented in the presence of creatine, and combined administration of creatine, methylglyoxal, and ascorbic acid provided greater efficacy and eliminated visible signs of tumor growth. Creatine and creatine kinase, very low in sarcoma tissue, were significantly elevated with concomitant regression of tumor cells.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine is reported to exert antioxidant effects, scavenging reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and stabilizing membranes, effects that are proposed to protect tissues from oxidative damage. Some studies suggest creatine supplementation reduces markers of oxidative stress and muscle damage after intense exercise, and experimental work indicates creatine can directly scavenge superoxide and peroxynitrite in vitro. Because oxidative stress contributes to DNA damage and tumor promotion, creatine's antioxidant capacity is cited in the trace as one possible mechanism for an anti-cancer effect, although direct evidence linking creatine's antioxidant action to cancer prevention in humans is lacking.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine supplementation is one of the most effective and best-documented ergogenic aids for improving performance in high-intensity, short-duration activities. By increasing muscle phosphocreatine stores, creatine enhances the capacity to regenerate ATP during repeated bouts of maximal exercise, increasing power output, strength gains during resistance training, and work performed in repeated sprint protocols. Meta-analyses consistently show moderate improvements in measures such as maximal strength, sprint performance, and lean body mass, with benefit most pronounced in activities relying on the phosphocreatine energy system. These well-established performance effects are the context in which the trace asks whether creatine also influences cancer outcomes.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine supplementation supports healthy glucose management by enhancing glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity. Mechanistically, creatine prevents the decline of GLUT4 during muscle disuse, increases GLUT4 during rehabilitation, and co-ingestion with carbohydrate or protein augments muscle creatine and glycogen. In individuals with type 2 diabetes, creatine supplementation during exercise training improved glucose tolerance to a standard meal, increased GLUT4 translocation, and lowered HbA1c, with AMPK signaling implicated in these effects. Creatine uptake into tissue is itself influenced by glucose and insulin, establishing a bidirectional relationship between creatine status and glycemic physiology that supports creatine as an adjunct for metabolic health.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine supplementation influences glucose handling in skeletal muscle, in part by upregulating the GLUT4 glucose transporter. Creatine prevents declines in GLUT4 during immobilization and increases GLUT4 by about 40% during rehabilitation after atrophy, and co-ingestion with carbohydrate and protein enhances creatine uptake and muscle glycogen. In type 2 diabetic patients, 12 weeks of creatine supplementation during training improved glucose tolerance, increased GLUT4 translocation, and significantly reduced HbA1c, with changes in AMPK signaling related to GLUT4 translocation and HbA1c. These findings indicate creatine enhances glucose uptake and supports glucose management, especially when combined with exercise.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine supplementation increases muscle creatine and phosphocreatine stores and, particularly when combined with resistance training, promotes gains in lean tissue mass and strength. Randomized trials in older adults show greater gains in muscle mass and isometric strength with creatine plus heavy resistance training compared to training alone, and meta-analyses confirm larger gains in muscle mass and upper-body strength in older individuals supplementing creatine during resistance exercise. Creatine also decreases protein breakdown and can preserve muscle mass during energy-restricted weight loss, making it a broadly useful strategy for maintaining muscle across the lifespan and in clinical rehabilitation populations.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine is a naturally occurring nitrogen-containing compound that is synthesized endogenously in the liver, kidney, and pancreas and is also obtained from dietary sources, particularly red meat and fish. Around 95 percent of the body's creatine is stored in skeletal muscle, approximately one-third of it in the phosphorylated form creatine phosphate. In the muscle it is converted to creatine phosphate, which donates its high-energy phosphate group to regenerate ATP from ADP, supporting short-duration, high-intensity exercise. Because of its role in ATP regeneration, creatine is one of the most widely used sports supplements and is increasingly examined for additional therapeutic effects, including possible anti-cancer properties.

subject: Creatine
context: Dietary creatine is obtained almost exclusively from animal-derived foods, with red meat and fish being the richest sources. Cooking does not destroy creatine, and an omnivorous diet typically supplies one to two grams of creatine per day, which complements the roughly one gram synthesized endogenously per day. Vegetarians have lower muscle creatine stores and show larger increases in response to supplementation than meat-eaters, reflecting the lower baseline intake. This dietary origin is relevant to epidemiologic questions about meat consumption and cancer risk, because creatine is often discussed alongside other meat-derived compounds when considering diet-cancer associations.

subject: Creatine
context: Within cells, creatine is phosphorylated by the enzyme creatine kinase to form creatine phosphate (phosphocreatine), which serves as a rapidly mobilizable reserve of high-energy phosphate. The reaction creatine plus ATP yields creatine phosphate plus ADP, and the reverse reaction regenerates ATP during bursts of high energy demand, such as muscle contraction. The phosphocreatine pool is the immediate energy buffer that sustains ATP levels for the first several seconds of maximal effort, before glycolysis and oxidative metabolism fully contribute. This conversion of creatine to creatine phosphate is the mechanistic heart of the creatine-phosphocreatine energy system.

subject: Creatine
context: Roughly two-thirds of the body's creatine pool is phosphorylated and stored as phosphocreatine (PCr), with the remainder held as free creatine. The creatine kinase (CK) reaction interconverts creatine and PCr, and the energy liberated by breaking PCr down into phosphate and creatine (about 10.3 kcal) is used to resynthesize ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This PCr/CK system is the rapid, phosphagen-based buffer that maintains ATP availability during intense exercise, ischemia, hypoxia, and high metabolic demand. Creatine supplementation raises muscle creatine and PCr stores, expanding this reserve and thereby enhancing high-intensity exercise capacity and training adaptations.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine monohydrate is among the most extensively studied dietary supplements and is generally regarded as safe when used at recommended doses over periods of many years. Long-term supplementation studies report no consistent adverse effects on renal, hepatic, or cardiovascular function in healthy individuals, and creatine is approved for use by many sports organizations. Common minor side effects include water retention and occasional gastrointestinal discomfort. This favorable safety profile is noted in the trace as relevant to the potential evaluation of creatine as an adjunct in oncology settings, where tolerability is a central concern.

subject: Creatine
context: Approximately 95 percent of the body's creatine is stored in skeletal muscle, where it exists partly as free creatine and partly as creatine phosphate. The muscle creatine pool is maintained by both endogenous synthesis and dietary intake, and it is depleted by high-intensity activity and resynthesized during recovery. Muscle total creatine concentrations can be increased by supplementation, typically by 10-20 percent, and this elevated store extends the time for which high-intensity exercise can be sustained. The predominance of skeletal muscle as a creatine depot explains why most creatine research has focused on muscle function, strength, and performance.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine is synthesized endogenously from the amino acids arginine, glycine, and methionine in a two-step pathway. The first step, catalyzed by arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT), takes place primarily in the kidney and pancreas and produces guanidinoacetate; the second step, catalyzed by guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT), transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to guanidinoacetate in the liver, producing creatine. This biosynthetic origin connects creatine metabolism to the methylation cycle and one-carbon metabolism, a connection relevant to hypotheses linking creatine status to epigenetic regulation and cancer risk.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine is a naturally occurring nitrogen-containing compound synthesized endogenously in the body. The first step of its biosynthesis condenses arginine and glycine into guanidinoacetate (GAA), a reaction catalyzed by arginine glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT), which is expressed in the kidney, pancreas, liver, and certain brain regions. Endogenous synthesis supplies roughly half of the daily creatine requirement; the remainder must come from the diet, primarily red meat and fish, or from supplements. Deficiencies in the enzymes of this pathway (AGAT, GAMT) or the creatine transporter produce creatine synthesis deficiency syndromes marked by low brain creatine and neurodevelopmental impairment.

subject: Creatine
context: Glycine serves as the second amino acid substrate for endogenous creatine synthesis. Arginine glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT) condenses arginine with glycine to produce guanidinoacetate (GAA), which is then methylated by guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT) using S-adenosyl methionine to yield creatine. Because glycine and arginine are the committed substrates for creatine biosynthesis, their availability influences the rate of endogenous creatine production, which normally covers about half of daily needs. The rest is obtained from dietary red meat, fish, or supplements, and total body creatine stores are typically around 120 mmol/kg of dry muscle mass.

subject: Creatine
context: Because endogenous creatine synthesis is the major consumer of methyl groups donated by S-adenosylmethionine, creatine status may influence DNA methylation reactions that govern gene expression, including the expression of oncogenes and tumor suppressors. Supplemental creatine, by reducing the requirement for de novo creatine synthesis, could preserve methyl groups for DNA methyltransferases and thereby modulate global DNA methylation patterns. The trace notes that this is an emerging and largely hypothesis-driven area: creatine's effects on DNA methylation and on one-carbon metabolism have been examined mainly in animal and small human studies, and any causal link to cancer prevention remains to be firmly established.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine and the creatine kinase system are increasingly studied in the context of cancer metabolism. Some cancer types, particularly those with a poor prognosis, upregulate creatine kinase isoenzymes, and creatine metabolism has been reported to support the growth and invasiveness of certain tumors, whereas in other contexts creatine appears to restrain tumor growth, possibly through effects on energy homeostasis and AMPK. The trace explicitly notes that creatine's relationship to cancer is context-dependent and that current evidence is insufficient to recommend creatine as an anti-cancer intervention, underscoring the need for direct experimental studies.

subject: Creatine
context: Emerging evidence reviewed in the source trace suggests creatine may exert direct anti-cancer effects, inhibiting tumorigenesis rather than only supporting athletic performance. Mechanistic studies indicate that creatine supplementation can raise cellular phosphocreatine and creatine kinase activity, and the resulting change in the cellular energy state, together with creatine-mediated effects on AMPK and anabolic signaling, may suppress cancer cell proliferation and transformation. Because cancer cells depend on high glycolytic flux and altered energy metabolism, interventions that perturb the creatine-phosphocreatine system are hypothesized to restrain tumor growth, although the trace stresses that much of this evidence is preliminary and requires confirmation in well-powered clinical studies.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine supplementation can alter the cellular energy status in ways that modulate AMPK, the central sensor of cellular energy charge. High phosphocreatine and low AMP levels generally suppress AMPK activation, while creatine depletion or energetic stress activates it. Because AMPK regulates anabolic processes, including protein synthesis and cell growth, and influences pathways relevant to cancer metabolism, creatine-induced changes in AMPK signaling are proposed to be one mechanism by which creatine could affect tumor cell proliferation. The trace presents this as a plausible but incompletely validated mechanistic link, noting that AMPK-dependent effects of creatine have been shown mainly in skeletal muscle and liver.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine supplementation has been investigated for its ability to attenuate muscle wasting in conditions of disuse, catabolism, and disease. In healthy subjects it amplifies the muscle gains from resistance training, and in some clinical populations, including elderly individuals and people with neuromuscular or catabolic diseases, creatine supplementation preserves lean mass and strength. Because cancer and its treatments frequently cause sarcopenia and cachexia, creatine's potential to blunt muscle loss is proposed as a supportive-care role for creatine in oncology, even if any direct anti-tumor effect remains unproven.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine and phosphocreatine play an important role in maintaining myocardial bioenergetics during ischemic events, reducing arrhythmias, ischemia-related damage, and improving heart function. Intravenous phosphocreatine prevented accumulation of arrhythmogenic lysophosphoglycerides in the ischemic zone of canine hearts, and adding phosphocreatine to cardioplegic solutions improved myocardial energy availability and reduced arrhythmias. Creatine supplementation also maintains energy availability during brain ischemia and reduces stroke-related damage. Several studies report benefits of oral creatine in chronic heart failure patients in rehabilitation, and phosphocreatine administration is considered a protective strategy for the heart during acute myocardial ischemia.

subject: Creatine
context: Preclinical studies suggest creatine supplementation can reduce the severity of spinal cord injury. Rats fed creatine before and after moderate spinal cord contusion developed less scar tissue and performed better on locomotor function tests than controls, and rats fed a 2% creatine diet before and after injury experienced less loss of gray matter. In humans with cervical spinal cord injury, creatine supplementation enhanced aerobic exercise capacity, ventilatory anaerobic threshold, and, combined with vitamin D and resistance training, improved arm muscle area, strength, and functional capacity. These findings support creatine as an adjunct that may reduce injury severity and enhance rehabilitation outcomes after spinal cord injury.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine supplementation has shown neuroprotective potential in traumatic brain injury. In animal models, providing creatine in the diet for 5 days prior to TBI decreased cortical brain damage by 36% in rats and 50% in mice, an effect attributed to improved energy availability in the injured brain. Creatine also reduces the severity of mild concussions and ischemic brain damage and improves learning and memory during recovery in neonatal mice. While these preclinical studies cannot be replicated in humans, they support the contention that creatine supplementation may reduce the severity of TBI and serve as an adjunctive strategy in individuals at risk of head injury, complementing its established role in muscle and rehabilitation settings.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine supplementation elevates brain creatine and phosphocreatine, improves brain bioenergetics, and has documented neuroprotective benefits, particularly in response to injury and ischemia. Animal studies show creatine feeding reduces cerebral ischemic brain damage volume by 25-40%, decreases infarct size, and attenuates neuronal death, while human studies report increased brain creatine (9.2% after 7 days), improved corticomotor excitability, and preserved attention during hypoxia. These findings suggest prophylactic creatine may reduce the severity of brain ischemia and stroke-related damage, and it has been investigated as a neuroprotective strategy in pregnancy to improve neonatal outcomes following birth asphyxia.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine provides the immediate phosphate group needed to recycle ADP back into ATP, the cellular energy currency, keeping cellular energy pools saturated and reducing metabolic stress, which protects HRV from plunging during hard training. It is recommended daily at 3-5 grams, ideally post-workout or with the largest carbohydrate meal, because creatine uptake is enhanced by insulin. Pairing creatine with carbohydrates and protein helps drive it into muscle and brain cells more efficiently, with consistency mattering more than exact timing.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine has immunomodulatory effects that include reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and other inflammatory markers like TNF-alpha and PGE2. A creatine-induced reduction of these inflammatory mediators may help explain some of the neuroprotective benefits observed in patients with central nervous system diseases and the attenuation of inflammatory and muscle damage markers after intense exercise. Creatine also down-regulates expression of toll-like receptors (TLR-2, TLR-3, TLR-4, TLR-7) in a mouse macrophage cell line and may influence cytokines through the NF-kB signaling pathway, with potential consequences for immune response and, notably, for TLR-4-mediated pathology in Parkinson's disease progression.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine acts as a direct and indirect antioxidant, in part by coupling to oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria. Creatine diffuses into mitochondria and, via mitochondrial creatine kinase, couples with ATP produced by oxidative phosphorylation and the adenine nucleotide translocator, after which phosphocreatine diffuses back into the cytosol. This coupling reduces the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) by keeping the mitochondrial adenine nucleotide pool well-adenylated and stabilizing electron transport. Consequently creatine supplementation is reported to lower oxidative stress markers, which may contribute to its protective effects on muscle, heart, and brain, particularly under ischemic or metabolically stressed conditions.

subject: Creatine
context: The primary biochemical function of creatine is to buffer cellular ATP levels through the creatine-phosphocreatine system. Creatine kinase reversibly catalyzes the transfer of a phosphoryl group from phosphocreatine to ADP, regenerating ATP at rates far exceeding mitochondrial or glycolytic ATP production, which is essential for short bursts of intense activity. The creatine kinase reaction therefore acts as a rapid temporal energy buffer, maintaining ATP:ADP ratios during muscle contraction and other energy-demanding processes. This ATP-regenerating capacity is the basis for creatine's ergogenic effects and is also central to hypotheses about its influence on cancer cell metabolism.

subject: Creatine
context: The biological actions of creatine are mediated by the creatine kinase enzyme family, which catalyzes the reversible phosphorylation of creatine by ATP. Tissue-specific creatine kinase isoforms are expressed in muscle, brain, and other tissues, and the enzyme couples the phosphocreatine pool to cellular ATP demand. In tissues with high and fluctuating energy requirements, the creatine kinase reaction buffers ATP levels and transports high-energy phosphate between sites of production and consumption. Because creatine kinase is also expressed in several tumors, the enzyme is a candidate interface through which creatine supplementation could influence cancer cell energy metabolism.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine and its related compound cyclocreatine have documented anticancer properties. Creatine is an important energy source for immune cells and supports CD8 T cell antitumor immunity, since creatine uptake via the SLC6A8 transporter regulates CD8 T cell function and creatine levels are low in malignant cells and antitumor T cells. Creatine also augments the efficacy of the anticancer medication methylglyoxal, with combined creatine, methylglyoxal, and ascorbic acid eliminating visible signs of tumor growth in experimental models. Evidence is emerging rather than definitive in humans, and creatine is being studied as an adjunct in cancer cachexia and treatment contexts.

subject: Creatine
context: High-dose, long-term creatine supplementation is a nutritional strategy for creatine synthesis deficiencies caused by mutations in AGAT, GAMT, or the creatine transporter (SLC6A8), which reduce endogenous creatine synthesis or cellular uptake and result in low brain creatine and phosphocreatine. Supplementation at 0.3-0.8 g/kg/day increases brain creatine and PCr levels and improves or stabilizes clinical symptoms including intellectual disability, epilepsy, and movement disorders. Patients with GAMT or AGAT deficiency treated early (e.g., starting at four months of age) can experience normal psychomotor development, and such therapy is well tolerated and may also benefit ornithine aminotransferase deficiency causing gyrate atrophy.

subject: Creatine
context: Creatine synthesis is the single largest consumer of S-adenosylmethionine-derived methyl groups in the body, using approximately 70 percent of available methyl donor flux. Guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to guanidinoacetate to form creatine, thereby competing with DNA methylation and other methylation reactions for the methyl pool. Because exogenous creatine supplementation reduces the demand for endogenous creatine synthesis, it can spare methyl groups and shift the balance of methylation reactions. This creatine-methionine interaction forms the mechanistic basis for the hypothesis that creatine could influence epigenetic processes relevant to cancer.

subject: Creatine Kinase (CK)
context: Creatine kinase (CK) is the enzyme at the core of the creatine/phosphocreatine energy system. It catalyzes the reversible transfer of a phosphate group between creatine and ADP, using the free energy released from phosphocreatine breakdown (approximately 10.3 kcal) to resynthesize ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This provides a rapid means of replenishing depleted ATP during high-energy-demand states such as intense exercise or conditions where energy production is impaired (ischemia, hypoxia) or insufficient due to increased demand (mental fatigue, disease states). Cytosolic, glycolytic, and mitochondrial CK isoforms cooperate to buffer ATP/ADP ratios and shuttle high-energy phosphate from mitochondria to sites of ATP consumption.

subject: Cross-linking
context: Cross-linking may be responsible for many of the problems of old age, including senile cataract, thickening of the arteries, some cancers and damage to the immune system. A damaged immune system leads to increased susceptibility to infection, and some cancers may arise from the effects of glucose on DNA, which can react with glucose to produce damaged DNA that causes abnormal cells to be produced. Aminoguanidine's ability to prevent cross-linking may help alleviate or prevent senile cataract as well as arterial thickening, kidney failure, thinning bones, osteoarthritis and skin wrinkles.

subject: CTPI2
context: CTPI2, a third-generation SLC25A1 inhibitor, delays the onset of frailty in aged mice as measured by a validated 31-parameter frailty index, alongside improvements in fur condition, coordination, balance and grip strength. In aged tissues, CTPI2 suppresses SASP-associated inflammatory gene expression across skeletal muscle, liver and heart while leaving p16 and p21 unchanged, and circulating inflammatory cytokines are reduced, indicating a systemic attenuation of inflammatory burden. These benefits arise without broad metabolic reprogramming: body weight, composition, metabolic rate, respiratory exchange ratio, activity and lipid metabolic pathways are largely unaffected.
source_document: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md

subject: CTPI2
context: Aged (19-month-old) C57BL/6 mice gavaged with CTPI2 (50 mg/kg three times weekly for 3 months) exhibited more lustrous fur, reduced alopecia and greying, and delayed onset of frailty as measured by a 31-parameter frailty index. Functional assessment revealed enhanced neuromuscular performance: improved coordination and balance (tightrope test), increased strength (hanging and grip strength tests) and preservation of muscle integrity. CTPI2 reduced SASP gene expression in skeletal muscle, liver and heart without altering p16 or p21, indicating that suppressing the mitochondrial citrate-acetyl-CoA axis improves healthspan through SASP modulation rather than senescent cell clearance.

subject: CTPI2
context: CTPI2 is a third-generation inhibitor of the mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1 with high binding affinity and specificity. CTPI2 treatment results in dose-dependent suppression of SASP components at transcript and protein levels without altering cell cycle regulators, HMGB1 localization, DNA damage foci or proliferation markers. It reduces global nuclear acetylation and H3K27ac at SASP loci and abolishes incorporation of glucose-derived carbon into histone acetylation, yet does not broadly impair mitochondrial function: OXPHOS gene expression, ATP production, coupling efficiency, mitochondrial ROS and morphology remain largely unchanged.

subject: DELE1
context: DELE1, previously identified as a poorly characterized mitochondrial protein from a yeast two-hybrid screen, was converged upon by two independent CRISPR-based screens as the mediator of mitochondrial stress signaling to the ISR. Under mitochondrial stress, the cleaved cytosolic fragment DELE1-S directly binds and activates the heme-regulated kinase HRI. Importantly, HRI activation by DELE1 was shown to be heme-independent, ruling out the classical heme-depletion mechanism. HRI activation in turn leads to eIF2alpha phosphorylation and downstream ATF4 induction, linking mitochondrial dysfunction to the integrated stress response.

subject: Diabetes Mellitus
context: Diabetes mellitus is often seen as a form of accelerated aging, and the levels of cross-linking products in diabetics are two to three times those of their equivalent normal non-diabetics. Advanced glycation end products are increased in diabetes and play an important role in the development of diabetic complications. Aminoguanidine acts to bind to sugars, preventing them from binding to the lysine groups of proteins, and diabetic clinical trials with humans have highlighted its ability to prevent oxidative modification of LDL, inhibit atherosclerotic plaque formation, reduce albuminuria and delay end-stage renal disease.
source_document: _document_ - Aminoguanidine An AGE Product Inhibitor  Antiaging Systems Articles.md

subject: DRP1
context: Cytosolic DRP1 monomers are recruited to the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) to initiate fission, where they are anchored by four main adaptor proteins: mitochondrial fission factor (MFF), mitochondrial fission 1 protein (FIS1), and mitochondrial dynamics proteins MID49 and MID51. These adaptors physically interact within a DRP1 complex to coordinate fission, and MFF, MID49 and MID51 are directly associated with mitochondrial division; their absence leads to significant mitochondrial elongation. The endoplasmic reticulum and ER-mitochondria contact sites (MAMs) provide a platform for DRP1 oligomerization and constriction of the OMM.
source_document: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md

subject: DRP1
context: DRP1 is recruited from the cytosol to defined sites on the mitochondrial outer membrane, where division occurs. Its adaptor proteins, including MFF, FIS1, MID49, and MID51, serve as receptors that concentrate DRP1 at prospective fission sites, often at positions where mitochondria are already constricted or associated with the endoplasmic reticulum. In cultured cells, MFF recruits DRP1 to the majority of fission events, while MID49 and MID51 recruit DRP1 to mitochondria independently of MFF in certain conditions. Once concentrated, DRP1 oligomerizes into spirals that wrap around the tubule, and GTP hydrolysis drives the membrane constriction required for complete scission.
source_document: _document_ - Mitochondrial Fusion and Fission The fine-tune balance for cellular homeostasis.md

subject: DRP1
context: Biochemical evaluation of Alzheimer's disease (AD) brains demonstrates significantly increased DRP1 and FIS1 and reduced MFN1, MFN2 and OPA1 mRNA and protein levels, correlating with mitochondrial fragmentation and compromised neuronal energy production. Excessive mitochondrial fission interferes with OXPHOS complex assembly and cristae integrity, and S-nitrosylation of DRP1 induced by amyloid beta triggers mitochondrial fission and neuronal damage. Significantly increased DRP1 phosphorylation at Ser616 stimulates DRP1 translocation to mitochondria and fission activity in AD brain, and impaired axonal transport and reduced mitophagy accompany AD progression.

subject: Epacadostat
context: Epacadostat is a small-molecule inhibitor of IDO1 tested in clinical trials as an immuno-oncology strategy, often in combination with checkpoint inhibitors targeting PD-1/PD-L1. These combinations aim to relieve IDO1-mediated immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment by blocking tryptophan depletion and kynurenine production, thereby restoring effector T cell function. However, results from such trials have been mixed, and challenges including isoform selectivity, compensatory pathways (TDO, IDO2), and context-specific effects have limited clinical success.

subject: Everolimus
context: Two randomized placebo-controlled clinical trials tested rapalogs among the elderly for immunomodulation. Treatment with everolimus monotherapy or everolimus in combination with RTB101 for six weeks resulted in a better response to influenza vaccine and fewer infections over the next year compared to placebo. The proposed mechanism is an increase in autophagy through inhibition of mTOR along with increased expression of antiviral proteins. The observation that immune function improves after a single six-week period of mTORC1 inhibition has important clinical implications, since elderly patients are particularly at risk of dying from influenza.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Everolimus
context: Everolimus, a rapamycin analog (rapalog), is FDA approved for anti-seizure therapy in tuberous sclerosis complex after many years of off-label use. The EXIST-3 multicenter phase III study evaluated adjunctive everolimus in patients with treatment-resistant epilepsy due to TSC and showed significant reduction in seizure frequency, with approximately 40% of patients in the high-dose group achieving at least a 50% reduction in seizures compared to only 15% in placebo. The success reflects TSC's clearly defined molecular etiology, with highly penetrant mutations driving mTOR hyperactivation making the pathway an actionable target.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption
context: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC), also known as the afterburn effect, is the elevated oxygen consumption that persists after an exercise session and represents the energy expended in excess of resting values during recovery. EPOC accounts for a portion of the total energy cost of exercise beyond the exercise itself, typically contributing an additional 7-15 percent of the exercise energy cost depending on intensity and duration. Because EPOC elevates the metabolic rate for hours after training, it is often cited to justify high-intensity training for weight management, although Speakman's analysis argues that the quantitative contribution to total daily expenditure is smaller than commonly claimed.

subject: Exercise
context: Exercise causes a transient but significant elevation of resting metabolic rate that outlasts the exercise bout itself. A number of studies show RMR is increased for at least 24-48 hours following vigorous exercise, and residual increases are detectable even up to 3 days after a single session in some protocols. The elevation appears largely independent of the intensity of the exercise, with high-intensity interval exercise providing comparable post-exercise energy expenditure to continuous moderate exercise when matched for work. This post-exercise elevation is one mechanism by which physical activity raises daily energy expenditure beyond the direct cost of the exercise itself.

subject: Exercise
context: Exercise raises total daily energy expenditure (TEE) through several mechanisms acting together: the direct metabolic cost of the exercise bout itself, the elevated resting metabolic rate and excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) that persist after the session, and increases in nonexercise activity thermogenesis and appetite in some individuals. Speakman uses doubly labelled water studies to show that while athletes have high TEE, the contribution of exercise to TEE in moderately active people is modest in magnitude, and that an exercise-induced rise in TEE of 10-15 percent is not necessarily compensated by reduced activity in other parts of the day.

subject: Exercise
context: Exercise is defined as planned, structured, and repetitive physical activity performed specifically to improve or maintain physical fitness, and it constitutes a subset of total physical activity, which also includes occupational activity, domestic activity, and non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT). In the energy balance framework of the Speakman review, exercise is the most flexible and controllable component of total daily energy expenditure, and its contribution to daily energy use is quantified through doubly labelled water studies. Because exercise is a voluntary component, it is the primary target of public-health interventions aimed at raising daily energy expenditure.

subject: Exercise
context: An important conclusion of the Speakman review is that exercise does not reliably increase appetite, and that in many individuals appetite is suppressed both during and for a period after exercise, an effect that can persist for up to 24 hours in some protocols. This is counter to the common belief that increased exercise necessarily drives increased food intake. When exercise does raise energy intake, the increase is generally smaller than the energy cost of the exercise, so a net negative energy balance is usually achieved. These findings support the view that exercise contributes to weight control by raising expenditure without a fully compensatory increase in intake.

subject: Exercise
context: Physical exercise is proposed as a low-cost, non-pharmacological means to stimulate mitohormesis. Rodent models show that exercise stimulates a UPRmt response in muscle and other tissues, and mitokines including GDF15 and MOTS-c are markedly stimulated by exercise, suggesting the potential to exploit these factors as exercise mimetics. However, too much exercise in humans actually impairs mitochondrial function, reduces ROS production, and worsens metabolic health, underscoring that the hormetic benefit of exercise depends on an appropriate dose and adequate recovery.

subject: Fasting
context: Intermittent fasting and time-restricted feeding compress the eating window to 8-10 hours to allow a 14-16 hour daily fasting period, described as the simplest and most effective way to activate AMPK and mitophagy. Constant snacking and chronic overeating abolish the fasting-induced AMPK signal necessary for mitophagy. Fasting-induced mitochondrial recycling is a core mitohormetic mechanism, and stopping food intake at least 3-4 hours before sleep is highlighted as a key variable that instantly improves overnight HRV by allowing the body to focus entirely on cellular repair during sleep.

subject: Fat Free Mass
context: Fat free mass (FFM) is the single best predictor of resting metabolic rate (RMR), explaining the majority of inter-individual variation in energy expenditure at rest. In the doubly labelled water and metabolic chamber studies reviewed by Speakman, FFM correlates with RMR with correlations typically above 0.7, with lean tissue contributing proportionally more than fat mass. The relationship reflects the high metabolic activity of lean tissues, especially the brain, liver, and skeletal muscle at rest. Consequently, any intervention that changes FFM, such as resistance training, is expected to alter RMR in proportion, though adaptive changes in metabolic efficiency can partially blunt this effect.

subject: Ferroptosis
context: Ferroptosis is a regulated, iron-dependent cell death pathway in which cells lose their ability to regulate fats and eventually die, as distinct from unregulated necrotic death or other programmed death programs like apoptosis. It was discovered and named (originally 'oxytosis') by Pam Maher in 2001. The hallmark mechanism is accumulation of lipid peroxides to toxic levels, normally kept in check by glutathione, and the pathway is increasingly linked to neurodegeneration and age-related diseases. Because ferroptosis is druggable and genetically regulatable, it has become a promising therapeutic target alongside cellular senescence for supporting healthy aging and clearing dysfunctional cells.

subject: Ferroptosis
context: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent cell death pathway in which the accumulation of lipid peroxides becomes toxic to cells. Pam Maher, the Salk senior author, discovered the pathway and named it (originally 'oxytosis') in 2001. Healthy cells keep lipid peroxides at steady levels with the help of glutathione, an antioxidant that can stave off ferroptosis. Ferroptosis has been increasingly linked to neurodegeneration - Maher's lab recently reported that chronic iron overexposure in neurons makes them less resilient over time and more vulnerable to neurodegeneration - and targeting the pathway has become a promising therapeutic strategy for age-related diseases alongside senescence research.
source_document: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md

subject: Ferroptosis
context: Ferroptosis is a regulated cell death pathway driven by the toxic accumulation of lipid peroxides. Cells die in ferroptosis when they lose the ability to regulate fats, and polyunsaturated fatty acids in membranes become the substrates for peroxidative damage. Healthy cells keep lipid peroxides at steady levels with the help of glutathione, an antioxidant that staves off ferroptosis. The pathway is iron-dependent and has been linked to aging and neurodegeneration, including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Understanding lipid-peroxide accumulation as the central executioner mechanism explains why membrane lipid remodeling - such as that caused by acid ceramidase - can sensitize cells to ferroptosis.
source_document: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md

subject: FGF21
context: FGF21 induces thermogenesis and promotes energy expenditure through UCP1-dependent mechanisms. FGF21 promotes thermogenic beiging of white adipose tissue, with protein restriction stimulating WAT beiging via FGF21 action in the brain through sympathetic signaling, and PR similarly increases thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue via an FGF21-dependent mechanism. These effects drive the increased energy expenditure observed with protein restriction and contribute to its metabolic benefits including reduced body weight and adiposity despite increased food intake. FGF21 also regulates lipid homeostasis, reducing circulating triglycerides, and mediates PR effects on senescence and inflammation in white adipose tissue.

subject: FGF21
context: FGF21 is essential for the longevity and many of the metabolic benefits of protein restriction. Fgf21-null mice do not live longer on PR, while mice overexpressing Fgf21 show ~30-40% lifespan extension, identifying FGF21 as the critical downstream mediator. FGF21 promotes energy expenditure in part through UCP1-dependent thermogenic beiging of white adipose tissue, acting in the brain through sympathetic signaling, and increases thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue. It also regulates lipid homeostasis, reduces circulating triglycerides, mediates PR effects on cellular senescence and inflammation in white adipose tissue, and reduces hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis in obese models.

subject: FIS1
context: FIS1 is a tail-anchored outer mitochondrial membrane protein that functions as a receptor for DRP1, helping to recruit the fission machinery to mitochondria. In yeast, the FIS1 ortholog Fis1p is the main membrane anchor for the Dnm1p fission GTPase, whereas in mammalian cells FIS1 plays a more accessory role alongside MFF, MID49, and MID51, and may also mediate non-DRP1 functions such as recruiting proteasomal and autophagic machinery to mitochondria. Overexpression of FIS1 fragments mitochondria, whereas FIS1 knockdown produces elongated networks, confirming its pro-fission role, although its relative importance varies between cell types and conditions.

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin is a potent antioxidant that scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species and stimulates endogenous antioxidant defenses including Nrf2-dependent expression of heme oxygenase-1, catalase, and superoxide dismutase. Its multiple hydroxyl groups allow it to donate electrons to quench free radicals and chelate metal ions that catalyze oxidative damage. The anti-oxidative action of fisetin underpins its protective effects in neuronal, cardiac, hepatic, and renal models of oxidative stress, and is considered a core mechanism shared with other polyphenols in its protective pharmacology.

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin is among the most extensively studied naturally occurring senolytics. It selectively eliminates senescent cells by inhibiting key pro-survival pathways, including the PI3K/Akt and Bcl-xL pathways that senescent cells depend on to resist apoptosis. In aged mice, a short course of oral fisetin reduced senescent cell burden in multiple tissues, extended healthspan and median lifespan, and alleviated age-related dysfunction. This senolytic activity distinguishes fisetin from many flavonoids and has driven its evaluation in human clinical trials for osteoarthritis, frailty, and other age-related conditions, though pharmacokinetic limitations remain a central obstacle.

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin shows broad anti-cancer activity against cell lines derived from lung, colon, breast, prostate, liver, melanoma, bladder, and leukemia. It inhibits cancer cell proliferation by arresting the cell cycle at G1 or G2/M phase, induces apoptosis through the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway with activation of caspases and modulation of Bcl-2 family proteins, and suppresses invasion and metastasis by inhibiting matrix metalloproteinases and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Fisetin also sensitizes tumor cells to conventional chemotherapeutics. Its anti-cancer efficacy in animal models, however, has been limited by the low concentrations achieved after oral dosing.

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin improves glucose homeostasis in experimental diabetes by enhancing insulin sensitivity and reducing hepatic glucose output. In diabetic rodents it lowers fasting blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin, reduces insulin resistance, and protects pancreatic beta cells, in part through its antioxidant activity and activation of AMPK signaling in liver and muscle. The review notes these metabolic benefits depend on adequate systemic exposure, which the oral delivery of unformulated fisetin may not achieve, further emphasizing the need for bioavailability-improving formulations to realize its therapeutic potential in humans.
source_document: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin is incompletely and variably absorbed after oral administration due to its low water solubility and rapid first-pass metabolism by intestinal and hepatic conjugating enzymes. Bioavailability studies report low and highly variable plasma fisetin concentrations after oral dosing, with most of the absorbed compound present as glucuronide and sulfate conjugates rather than the parent aglycone. The review identifies this limited oral absorption as the principal barrier to clinical translation of fisetin's broad preclinical pharmacology, and the majority of the formulation strategies it discusses are specifically aimed at increasing the fraction of the orally administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged.
source_document: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin has extremely low water solubility, reported in the range of a few micrograms per milliliter, which classifies it as a Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS) class II or IV drug. The low solubility, combined with poor permeability in some assessments and extensive intestinal and hepatic first-pass metabolism, results in low and erratic oral bioavailability. Because dissolution is the rate-limiting step for oral absorption, much of the formulation research described in the review aims to increase the dissolution rate and apparent solubility of fisetin, using approaches such as solid dispersions, cyclodextrin inclusion complexes, and nanocrystals.
source_document: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin exerts neuroprotective effects that are attributed to its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and direct signaling actions in neurons. It protects cultured neurons from oxidative and excitotoxic insults, and in animal models of ischemia and Parkinson's disease it reduces neuronal loss and improves motor function. Fisetin also acts as a cognitive enhancer, improving learning and memory in healthy rodents through modulation of ERK-CREB signaling and by promoting synaptic plasticity, and it has been proposed as a candidate for Alzheimer's disease based on its ability to reduce beta-amyloid aggregation and tau pathology. These effects motivate delivery strategies aimed at improving brain exposure.

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin suffers from intrinsically poor bioavailability that restricts its clinical translation. Its water solubility is very low (below 10 ug/mL), and the compound is sensitive to light, heat, and oxidative degradation. After oral administration fisetin is rapidly metabolized in the gut and liver to glucuronide and sulfate conjugates, so systemic exposure of the parent compound is minimal. The review documents that oral fisetin has short half-life and low plasma concentrations, and it attributes these problems to the BCS class II/IV characteristics of fisetin, motivating the development of macro- and nano-formulations to improve its absorption.
source_document: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin targets the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-xL, which is overexpressed in many cancer cells and in senescent cells as a survival mechanism. By inhibiting Bcl-xL and the related pro-survival pathways PI3K/Akt, fisetin lowers the threshold for apoptosis, promoting the death of senescent cells and chemoresistant cancer cells. The reliance of senescent cells on Bcl-xL is precisely the vulnerability that senolytics exploit, and fisetin's capacity to inhibit Bcl-xL is a key mechanistic basis for its senolytic activity and for its ability to sensitize tumors to existing therapies.
source_document: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin suppresses inflammation through multiple converging mechanisms. It inhibits the NF-kB pathway, reducing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6, and it inhibits cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) and inducible nitric oxide synthase, decreasing prostaglandin and nitric oxide levels. It also blocks the STAT1 and STAT3 signaling cascades that amplify inflammatory gene expression. These anti-inflammatory actions contribute to fisetin's protective effects in arthritis, colitis, acute lung injury, and neuroinflammation models, and the anti-inflammatory activity is preserved in some nanoformulations of the compound.
source_document: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin belongs to the pharmacological class of senolytics, agents that selectively kill senescent cells. Senolytics, exemplified by fisetin and dasatinib plus quercetin, exploit the reliance of senescent cells on anti-apoptotic survival networks. Fisetin's senolytic profile was identified in screening studies and validated in mouse models where it cleared senescent cells in adipose tissue, bone marrow, and other organs and extended healthspan. Because senescent cell accumulation drives tissue dysfunction and age-related disease, fisetin is now being evaluated in human trials, and its classification as a senolytic frames the therapeutic rationale for improving its bioavailability.
source_document: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin (3,3',4',7-tetrahydroxyflavone) is a natural flavonoid of the flavonol subclass found in strawberries, apples, persimmons, onions, and cucumbers, with strawberries being the richest dietary source. It has the molecular formula C15H10O6 and a molecular weight of 286.24 g/mol. Fisetin is widely studied as a senolytic agent, and its anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer, anti-diabetic, and neuroprotective activities are reported in numerous in vitro and in vivo studies. Despite its broad pharmacological potential, fisetin has extremely poor aqueous solubility, which severely limits its oral bioavailability.

subject: Fisetin
context: Once absorbed, fisetin is extensively conjugated by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs) and sulfotransferases in the intestinal epithelium and liver, producing fisetin glucuronide and fisetin sulfate metabolites that circulate in the plasma. Because these conjugates have reduced biological activity and are rapidly excreted via bile and urine, the parent aglycone fisetin reaches only low concentrations in tissues. The extent of this phase II metabolism is a primary cause of fisetin's poor oral bioavailability and short plasma half-life, and it is one reason most preclinical efficacy studies have used intraperitoneal injection rather than oral dosing.
source_document: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin regulates the PI3K/Akt pathway, which is central to both its anti-cancer and senolytic activities. In cancer cells, fisetin suppresses Akt phosphorylation and downstream mTOR signaling, reducing proliferation and survival, whereas in the context of senescence, fisetin's inhibition of PI3K/Akt removes a survival signal that senescent cells rely on, triggering their elimination. Fisetin's modulation of this pathway is dose-dependent and context-dependent, and it also crosstalks with MAPK/ERK signaling. Nanoformulations designed to raise fisetin exposure are expected to amplify these pathway-level effects by delivering higher intracellular concentrations.

subject: Fisetin
context: Fisetin clears senescent cells from tissues, reducing the burden of cellular senescence that accumulates with aging. In naturally aged and progeroid mice, oral fisetin lowered the number of p16INK4a-positive and SA-beta-galactosidase-positive cells in adipose tissue, skin, and other organs, and improved age-related tissue pathology. By removing senescent cells, fisetin also reduces the pro-inflammatory secretory phenotype they maintain, which contributes to age-related chronic inflammation. The capacity of fisetin to reduce cellular senescence in vivo is the defining action of its senolytic pharmacology and the basis for its proposed healthspan benefits.

subject: FUNDC1
context: FUNDC1 (FUN14 domain containing 1) is an outer mitochondrial membrane protein that serves as a mitophagy receptor for hypoxia-induced mitophagy, interacting directly with LC3 after dephosphorylation by phosphoglycerate mutase 5. ULK1 interacts with FUNDC1 and phosphorylates it at serine 17, enhancing FUNDC1 binding to LC3, and FUNDC1 interacts with OPA1 and DRP1 in a manner regulated by serine 13 phosphorylation during hypoxia or membrane potential loss. DRP1 can interact with overexpressed FUNDC1 to facilitate mitochondrial fragmentation and Parkin-mediated mitophagy.

subject: GCN2
context: GCN2 is an evolutionarily conserved stress-responsive serine/threonine kinase activated by amino acid restriction through uncharged tRNAs, as well as by ribosome stalling and collision. Activated GCN2 phosphorylates eIF2alpha, which suppresses global protein synthesis while selectively promoting translation of ATF4, a key transcription factor that activates stress response and autophagy genes. This selective translation of ATF4 is a central feature of the integrated stress response engaged during protein restriction. Genetic evidence confirms GCN2's importance: Drosophila lacking Gcn2 die when amino acids are restricted, deletion of Gcn2 in yeast blocks dietary restriction lifespan extension, and GCN2 overexpression extends lifespan in both organisms.

subject: GCN2
context: Tryptophan depletion caused by IDO1 activity activates the GCN2 stress kinase, which leads to cell cycle arrest, anergy, or apoptosis in effector T cells, since tryptophan is essential for T cell proliferation. This amino-acid starvation response is one of the two main mechanisms of IDO1-mediated immunosuppression, the other being kynurenine/aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling that promotes regulatory T cells. Together these pathways create an immunosuppressive microenvironment exploited by tumors, and this biology is the rationale for IDO1 inhibitors in immuno-oncology: blocking tryptophan catabolism is intended to relieve GCN2-driven T cell suppression and restore antitumor immunity.

subject: Ghrelin
context: The metabolic hormone ghrelin, a major regulator of food intake, also exerts immunomodulatory and thymopoietic effects. Ghrelin binds immune cell subsets via ghrelin-specific receptors and localizes to lipid rafts of activated T cells. Dixit et al. reported that ghrelin reduces age-associated inflammatory responses in mice, and in aged thymus both ghrelin and growth hormone levels decrease in correlation with functional thymic involution and elevated inflammation.

subject: Ghrelin
context: Ghrelin reduces age-associated inflammatory responses in mice. In the aged thymus, ghrelin and growth hormone levels decrease and correlate with functional thymic involution and generalized elevated inflammation, implying that the decline of these hormones contributes to the age-associated inflammatory milieu. In addition to suppressing inflammation, ghrelin has a stimulatory effect on thymus cellularity, increasing early thymic progenitors and recent thymic emigrants.

subject: Glutathione
context: Glutathione, an antioxidant, keeps lipid peroxides at steady levels and thereby staves off ferroptosis in healthy cells. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent cell death pathway in which the accumulation of lipid peroxides becomes toxic, and glutathione's antioxidant capacity is the canonical defense against this form of death. The Salk study's discovery is notable because the acid ceramidase axis sensitizes cells to ferroptosis without involving changes in glutathione levels, operating instead through lipid metabolism - an entirely novel, GPX4/GSH-independent pathway. This contrasts with the classical view that ferroptosis sensitivity is controlled chiefly by glutathione/GPX4-dependent peroxide neutralization.

subject: Glycation
context: Glycation is the product of the reaction between a sugar and the free amino group of proteins, referred to as cross-linking, and the accumulation of these glycation byproducts results in large, cross-linked molecules that inhibit the ability of the cell to function normally. Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) accumulate with age in tissues, contributing to arterial stiffening and cardiac enlargement. Levels of cross-linking products in diabetics are two to three times those of non-diabetics, and AGEs are believed to play an important role in the development of diabetic complications.

subject: HAF-1
context: HAF-1 is an inner mitochondrial membrane ABC-transporter family protein in C. elegans that exports matrix-derived peptides into the cytosol to signal mitochondrial stress. Proteins degraded by matrix proteases generate peptides that exit the mitochondria through HAF-1 (analogous to the yeast Mdl1 transporter), and this peptide release triggers a nuclear transcriptional response involving the ubiquitin-like protein UBL-5, the homeobox transcription factor DVE-1, and ATFS-1. The mechanism is reminiscent of peptide-based quorum sensing in gram-positive bacteria, where peptides exported via ABC transporters activate two-component histidine kinase sensors.

subject: Heart Rate Variability
context: HRV is highly individual and a universal normal range does not exist; factors such as age, sex, health conditions, and activity levels all shape an individual's baseline. General adult ranges only serve as rough guidelines, and HRV declines with age. More important than any single raw number is an individual's personal baseline trend: a sustained drop of 20 percent or more in average HRV is a far more insightful signal than a specific value on a standardized chart, making trends over 3 to 7 days the practical unit of analysis.

subject: Heart Rate Variability
context: HRV is directly controlled by the autonomic nervous system, which has two main branches with opposing effects. The sympathetic nervous system, the fight-flight-freeze system, releases adrenaline and cortisol that force the heart to beat faster and more rhythmically, lowering HRV. The parasympathetic nervous system, the rest-digest-and-repair system controlled heavily by the vagus nerve, allows more fluctuation between heartbeats, raising HRV. A high HRV therefore reflects strong vagal tone and a cardiovascular system that is highly responsive and flexible, while low HRV signals chronic stress, fatigue, or illness.

subject: Honokiol
context: Honokiol enhances the phosphorylation and activity of Akt, a central pro-survival kinase. In senescence-accelerated mice, oral honokiol (1 mg/kg) prevented age-related memory and learning deficits by preserving cholinergic neurons and enhancing Akt phosphorylation, part of the pro-survival PI3K/Akt pathway. Akt activation contributes to honokiol's neuroprotective effects against ischemia, beta-amyloid toxicity, and other insults, complementing its GABA-A modulation, Na+/K+-ATPase preservation, and anti-inflammatory actions.

subject: Honokiol
context: Honokiol attenuates inflammatory pain, reducing formalin-induced paw-licking behavior in the inflammatory phase and thermal hyperalgesia in mice. It blocks nociceptive signaling evoked by NMDA, glutamate, substance P, and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), and decreases formalin-induced c-Fos protein expression in superficial laminae (I-II) of the L4-L5 lumbar dorsal horn. Compared with magnolol, honokiol is more selective for NMDA-induced behavioral responses and hyperalgesia. Its analgesic effects are multifactorial, involving both the inflammatory cascade and glutamatergic/NMDA receptor pathways.
