In Drosophila, PR increases resilience during aging, improving responses to starvation, bacterial infection, and heat stress. Randomized controlled trials in humans show low-protein diets reduce body weight, fat mass, and fasting blood glucose, improve insulin sensitivity, and reduce inflammation, supporting PR as a practical alternative to calorie restriction for healthy aging.

subject: Protein Restriction
context: Protein restriction increases energy expenditure, in part through FGF21-mediated mechanisms. FGF21 promotes energy expenditure through UCP1-dependent thermogenic beiging of white adipose tissue, with PR stimulating WAT beiging via FGF21 action in the brain through sympathetic signaling, and PR similarly increases thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue via an FGF21-dependent mechanism. The increased energy expenditure drives increased food intake with PR by shifting brain signaling toward protein appetite. These effects occur despite, and in part explain, the paradox that PR improves metabolic health while increasing food intake, and they are most pronounced in males but also present in females and effective even when initiated late in life.

subject: Protein Restriction
context: Protein restriction couples autophagy activation with translation suppression, an adaptive response to amino acid scarcity that preserves cellular homeostasis. Upon mTORC1 inhibition, ULK1 initiates autophagosome formation, and mice lacking hepatic autophagy activation have blunted responses to PR. Amino acid sensing is physiologically important because scarcity promotes catabolic pathways and induces autophagy, allowing recycling of cellular components during dietary restriction. The coordinated response to PR thus requires the activation of GCN2 and inhibition of mTORC1, which together shift the cell from growth and translation toward proteostatic maintenance and nutrient recycling, contributing to the healthspan and longevity benefits of PR.

subject: Protein Restriction
context: FGF21 is the primary endocrine mediator of protein restriction's metabolic benefits. PR robustly elevates FGF21 in mice, rats, and humans, and FGF21 is required for many of PR's effects - increased food intake, reduced body weight, increased energy expenditure, and extended lifespan. Other geroprotective diets including calorie restriction, methionine restriction, BCAA restriction, and isoleucine restriction also induce FGF21. Mice overexpressing Fgf21 show ~30% (males) and ~40% (females) lifespan extension, while Fgf21-null mice do not live longer on PR. FGF21 also suppresses senescence and inflammation in white adipose tissue and reduces hepatic steatosis and fibrosis in obese models.

subject: Protein Restriction
context: Protein restriction inhibits the master nutrient sensor mTORC1 in the liver, heart, muscle, adipose tissue, and brain, and this inhibition is required for PR's benefits - without it, the benefits are lost. mTORC1 inhibition suppresses protein synthesis by reducing phosphorylation of S6K1 (whose genetic ablation extends lifespan) and of 4E-BP1, blocking eIF4E from initiating translation, while simultaneously promoting autophagy via ULK1 initiation of autophagosome formation. Normal aging is characterized by constitutive mTORC1 activation in many tissues, whereas pharmacological or genetic inhibition of mTORC1 extends lifespan in many species. Amino acid scarcity is sensed in part through leucine signaling to mTORC1 in specific neurons via a voltage-gated calcium channel (Cav3.1).

subject: Protein Restriction
context: Protein restriction reduces adiposity while increasing energy expenditure, an effect that occurs despite increased food intake. In young and aged rodents, PR reduces body fat, increases energy expenditure, and improves glucose homeostasis, with effects most pronounced in males but also present in females, and it remains effective when initiated late in life (18-20 months). These metabolic benefits are largely mediated by FGF21, which promotes energy expenditure through UCP1-dependent thermogenic beiging of white adipose tissue and increases thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue, shifting brain signaling toward protein appetite. Randomized controlled trials confirm low-protein diets reduce body weight and fat mass in humans despite increased caloric intake.

subject: Protein Restriction
context: Protein restriction reduces cellular senescence, one of its six defined hallmarks. High-protein diets increase hepatic senescence and SASP, increase inflammation and senescence in white adipose tissue (reduced by PR through an FGF21-dependent mechanism), and promote senescent cell accumulation in the kidney, whereas PR reduces these burdens. FGF21 itself suppresses senescence in cultured cells, reducing drug-induced senescence and pro-inflammatory SASP markers. Isoleucine and valine restriction likewise reduce hepatic senescence and SASP. Because senescent cells drive tissue dysfunction and accelerate aging, PR's suppression of senescence represents a core mechanism linking dietary protein intake to healthspan.

subject: Protein Restriction
context: Protein restriction blunts age-associated increases in frailty, a state of vulnerability increasing risk of dependency, falls, hospitalization, and mortality. In mice, PR reduced frailty while extending lifespan (34.9% increase in males on a 21% vs 7% protein diet), and isoleucine and valine restriction likewise reduce frailty and extend healthspan. The relationship between protein and frailty is complex: some observational studies associate higher protein intake with reduced frailty risk, but a British twin study showed more protein is associated with increased sarcopenia risk, while a low-protein Mediterranean diet was associated with increased muscle mass and strength, and plant but not animal protein is associated with reduced frailty risk. Exercise can largely offset lean mass loss on low-protein diets.

subject: Protein Restriction
context: Protein restriction reduces systemic and tissue inflammation. In white adipose tissue, high-protein diets increase inflammation and senescence while PR reduces both through an FGF21-dependent mechanism. Randomized controlled trials in humans show low-protein diets reduce inflammatory markers and lower insulin, hemoglobin A1C, and kidney disease outcomes in diabetic patients. High circulating branched-chain amino acids are associated with obesity, insulin resistance, and inflammation, whereas BCAA restriction reduces hepatic cellular senescence and improves metabolic health. These anti-inflammatory effects complement PR's other hallmarks and contribute to reduced risk of age-related diseases such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and cancer associated with high-protein diets.

subject: Proton Leak
context: Mitochondrial proton leak, the passive return of protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane that bypasses ATP synthase, is a significant component of resting metabolic rate and of the energy expenditure of skeletal muscle. Because proton leak uncouples oxygen consumption from ATP production, it dissipates a portion of the proton gradient as heat and is estimated to account for roughly 20 percent of resting oxygen consumption in mammals. Speakman discusses how variations in proton leak, partly set by the expression of uncoupling proteins such as UCP3 in muscle, contribute to inter-individual differences in metabolic rate and, potentially, to differences in exercise-induced energy expenditure.

subject: PTEN
context: PTEN is the main phosphatase that indirectly inactivates PI3K in the mTOR-PI3K signaling cascade, providing the antagonistic deactivating arm that balances PI3K activation. Alongside PP2A, which counteracts the effect of mTORC1 in the activation of S6K1/2, PTEN is one of the two key phosphatases modeled as kinase-phosphatase opposing pairs. The balance between activating and deactivating reactions at key nodes, such as the positive correlation between activation and deactivation of mTORC2, is consistent with the requirement for opposite reactions to underlie biphasic dose-responses.

subject: Rapamycin
context: Autophagy is strongly regulated by the mTORC1 complex, which inhibits autophagy initiation by blocking the ULK1 complex under conditions of nutrient abundance. Rapamycin's inhibition of mTORC1 cancels this effect by activating autophagy and supporting amino acid recycling and the removal of damaged structures. With age, autophagy activity decreases, leading to accumulation of damaged mitochondria and proteins. In many model organisms from yeast to mammals, mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin restores autophagic activity and increases lifespan, and long-term administration increases autophagy, reduces lipofuscin accumulation, and improves cardiomyocyte function.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin binds specifically and reversibly to mTORC1, the rapamycin-sensitive complex formed when mTOR associates with raptor; the downstream readout of the signaling cascade in this study is instead mTORC2. Long-term rapamycin exposure (around 24 hours) traps mTOR in mTORC1 complexes, and this sequestration obstructs the assembly of mTORC2. Because rapamycin acts as an indirect activator of mTORC2 via PI3K and an indirect inhibitor of mTORC2 through this sequestration, the pathway architecture resembles an incoherent bivalent network motif centered on the target mTORC1.

subject: Rapamycin
context: While aspirin may cause gastric ulceration and bleeding, rapamycin may cause stomatitis and mucositis, ulceration of the mucous membranes of the mouth and digestive tract, when used at high doses or chronically. A rare side effect of rapamycin is noninfectious interstitial pneumonitis, and by inhibiting neutrophil function rapamycin may increase the severity of bacterial infections. These side effects require rapamycin's discontinuation, but for anti-aging purposes rapamycin may be used intermittently (e.g., once a week) or at low daily doses and can be discontinued if any unpleasant effects occur.

subject: Rapamycin
context: At high doses rapamycin and everolimus slow cell proliferation, which decreases blood cell counts and results in mild and reversible thrombocytopenia, anemia and leukopenia as their most common side effects. A mild reduction of platelets may actually be beneficial, since one of the intended effects of aspirin is a decrease in platelet function. These reversible side effects contrast with the irreversible and inevitable effects of aging such as cancer, stroke, infarction, blindness and premature death, and can be avoided by intermittent scheduling or low-dose administration.

subject: Rapamycin
context: In aging models, mTOR inhibition by rapamycin is associated with increased autophagy, reduced cellular senescence and delayed aging. Rapamycin reduces markers of senescence in human skin in an exploratory randomized trial, and mid-life administration delays onset of age-related pathologies in mice. In contrast with its robust effects in monogenic mTORopathies where the molecular etiology is clearly defined, aging is a heterogeneous, multifactorial process without a single dominant pathway, which may explain why mTOR inhibition yields robust disease-modifying effects in epilepsy models but inconsistent outcomes in aging research.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin is arguably the most widely reported hormetic drug, an FDA-approved macrolide antibiotic used clinically for immunosuppression in organ-transplant patients and for certain cancers and autoimmune conditions. Many independent studies show a clear inverted U-shaped dose-response curve after long-term rapamycin inhibition (more than 24 hours of treatment) in terms of cell viability, mitochondrial density and Ki-67 expression, with maximum efficiency typically around 1 nM and reduced effects at higher concentrations up to 50 nM. The study proposes that this hormesis arises from the network topology of the mTOR-PI3K signaling cascade rather than from side effects or cytotoxicity alone.

subject: Rapamycin
context: In one short-lived mutant strain of mice, the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin (known clinically as sirolimus) extends maximum life span nearly three-fold. Rapamycin also prolongs life in normal mice as well as in yeast, worms and flies, and prevents age-related conditions in rodents, dogs, nonhuman primates and humans. In two dozen studies using different strains of mice, rapamycin extended life span, starting from the thorough study by Harrison and colleagues; rapamycin and its analog everolimus are FDA-approved for human use and have been used safely for decades, and rapamycin extends lifespan even when started late in life.

subject: Rapamycin
context: Inhibition of mTOR through rapamycin and its analogs (rapalogs) consistently prolongs life in numerous animal models while improving age-related physiological functions. The breakthrough occurred in 2009 when rapamycin was reported to extend the life of genetically heterogeneous mice, changing the scientific world's perception of aging. Subsequent studies showed rapamycin extends median lifespan by about 10% in UM-HET3 mice and improves glucose tolerance, frailty indicators, gait speed, liver parameters, and weight, while in Drosophila it extends lifespan through increased autophagy and decreased age-related intestinal pathologies. Rapamycin was the only drug among five tested that altered survival.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: In a study of 24 middle-aged companion dogs, echocardiography showed improvements in both diastolic and systolic measures of age-related cardiac function (E/A ratio, fractional shortening, and ejection fraction) in dogs treated with rapamycin. Rapamycin also stimulates the breakdown of damaged cytoplasmic elements, reduces oxidative stress, and supports tissue regeneration in cardiac tissue, and induces production of growth factors IGF1 and VEGF while reducing IL-1beta and TNF-alpha to support cardiac regeneration after infarction. Cardiovascular diseases are the main cause of death in the elderly, making mTOR inhibitors a promising direction for cardioprotective research.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: At anti-aging doses rapamycin eliminates hyperimmunity rather than suppressing immunity, or more figuratively rejuvenates immunity, enabling rapamycin and everolimus to act as immunostimulators that improve immunity in cancer patients and the elderly. Rapamycin reduces the risk of CMV infection in organ transplant patients, improves antipathogen and anticancer immunity in mice, prolongs lifespan in infection-prone mice and protects aged mice against pneumonia. Rapamycin also inhibits viral replication, including replication of the 1918 flu virus by 100-fold, and protects against lethal influenza infection when administered during vaccination.

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin improves the NAD+/NADH redox balance, which supports normal oxidative phosphorylation and reduces cellular pseudohypoxia associated with mTOR hyperactivity and HIF-1alpha accumulation. As a result, lactate production is reduced and cellular energy efficiency improves. In addition, inhibition of mTOR promotes mitochondrial biogenesis and increases the expression of key regulators such as PGC-1alpha and mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), leading to renewal of mitochondrial populations and improved fatty acid metabolism in senescent tissues including the myocardium and brown adipose tissue.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: The mTORC1 pathway controls mRNA translation, and its overactivity increases the rate of protein synthesis at the expense of protein quality. Inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin reduces translation, improves its accuracy, and promotes longer life by reducing genetic code reading errors and the accumulation of abnormal proteins, a mechanism confirmed in Drosophila and C. elegans models. Rapamycin also inhibits cap-dependent translation of mRNA, supporting alternative stress-resistant translation that increases production of stress-response and mitochondrial-protection proteins such as HSP70 and TFAM, and by activating ATF4 and producing hydrogen sulfide it increases resistance to oxidative stress.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: The mTOR pathway plays a key role in immunity, and its inhibition by rapamycin can restore immune balance. Rapamycin reduces lymphocyte overactivation and the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-4 and TNFalpha while increasing the number of regulatory T cells (Tregs). Inhibition of mTORC1 reduces chronic inflammation by decreasing the activity of the NF-kappaB pathway and the NLRP3 inflammasome complex, reducing production of IL-1beta and IL-18 cytokines and reducing leukocyte infiltration. The immune effects are dose-dependent, with lower doses immunostimulatory and higher doses immunosuppressive.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin's purported geroprotective effects are often attributed to its ability to induce autophagy, the cellular recycling process responsible for degrading protein aggregates and other damage-associated molecular patterns. mTORC1 normally inhibits autophagy by phosphorylating components of the ULK1 (Unc-51-like autophagy-activating kinase 1) complex, and its inhibition by rapamycin removes this suppression and initiates autophagosome formation. However, autophagy is context-dependent in cancer: while it may suppress tumor initiation by clearing damaged components, it can also support the survival and growth of established tumors.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Chronic rapamycin treatment is associated with metabolic disturbances including glucose intolerance and hyperlipidemia in both mice and humans administered rapamycin for prevention of immunosenescence. Mechanistically these effects are attributed not only to mTORC1 inhibition but also to unintended suppression of mTORC2, which induces insulin resistance - a mechanistic trade-off between metabolic side effects and longevity benefits. Houde et al. showed chronic rapamycin causes glucose intolerance and hyperlipidemia by upregulating hepatic gluconeogenesis and impairing lipid deposition in adipose tissue.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Chronic rapamycin or everolimus use is associated with elevated cholesterol and triglyceride levels (hyperlipidemia), alongside mucosal ulcers, impaired wound healing, delayed tissue repair, and increased infection risk. These metabolic disturbances were common in the EXIST-3 trial and other cohorts, along with stomatitis, infections, and cytopenias. The mechanisms are attributed to both mTORC1 inhibition and unintended mTORC2 suppression, which induces insulin resistance.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin can be viewed as a partial starvation-mimetic, and prolonged treatment may lead to the emergence of starvation pseudo-diabetes (SPD), a reversible, benign metabolic state resembling fasting that includes insulin resistance, glucose intolerance and mild hyperglycemia. SPD is reversible and does not lead to complications, and rapamycin reduces the incidence of diabetic complications such as diabetic nephropathy in rodents. In healthy elderly humans chronic treatment with rapamycin or everolimus did not cause hyperglycemia, and rapamycin-induced SPD can be avoided by intermittent or lower-dose administration and reversed by drug discontinuation.

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin, also called sirolimus, is an organic chemical compound produced by Streptomyces hygroscopicus, isolated from soil samples taken on Easter Island Rapa Nui by Georges Nogrady in the late 1960s. At the molecular level it acts as a specific inhibitor of mTOR by forming a complex with the immunophilin FKBP12, which then binds to mTOR and suppresses its kinase activity. As a result, rapamycin downregulates protein synthesis, cell growth, and anabolic metabolism while promoting autophagy, shifting the cell from anabolic to maintenance and repair processes, a key mechanism underlying its longevity-promoting effects.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin, an antibiotic discovered in the 1970s from Streptomyces hygroscopicus on Easter Island (Rapanui), inhibits mTORC1, the master kinase within the mTOR pathway that regulates cell growth, protein synthesis, and metabolism. By inhibiting mTORC1, rapamycin mimics the biochemistry of nutrient scarcity achieved by caloric restriction, shifting cellular activity from anabolic processes toward maintenance and repair pathways, promoting autophagy and improved proteostasis. mTORC1 activity increases with age, contributing to age-related pathologies, so its inhibition is theorized to slow aging.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin-induced mTORC2 inhibition has been shown to induce insulin resistance, highlighting a mechanistic trade-off between metabolic side effects and longevity benefits. While rapamycin's canonical target is mTORC1, chronic exposure also suppresses mTORC2, and this unintended suppression - rather than mTORC1 inhibition alone - mediates the glucose intolerance and insulin resistance observed in mice and humans. Lamming et al. demonstrated that rapamycin-induced insulin resistance is mediated by mTORC2 loss and is uncoupled from longevity.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin has emerged as a leading caloric restriction mimetic because its effects converge on the same nutrient-sensing pathways engaged by reduced nutrient intake. Caloric restriction has extended lifespans across yeast, flies and rodents, with significant results in primates, though evidence in humans is unclear. Suppression of mTORC1 by rapamycin reproduces the biochemistry of nutrient scarcity, and is theorized to shift cells from anabolic processes toward maintenance and repair, promoting autophagy and improved proteostasis - mechanisms associated with lifespan extension.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin is a natural anti-fungal antibiotic produced by soil bacteria of Eastern Island whose patent has expired, and pharmacological companies have developed other rapalogs such as everolimus. The term rapalogs encompasses rapamycin, everolimus and any other analogs, and at equipotent doses rapamycin and everolimus exert almost identical therapeutic and adverse effects, although everolimus is weaker and has a shorter half-life. All current rapalogs exhibit the same side effects as rapamycin and everolimus, and their real side effects are mTORC1-dependent.

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin and its analogs are metabolized by the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP3A4 and are therefore sensitive to pharmacokinetic drug interactions. Cannabidiol (CBD) is a potent CYP3A inhibitor that increases circulating levels of mTOR inhibitors, raising the risk of toxicity - a clinically relevant interaction given the widespread use of CBD and other cannabis products. This has been documented in patients with tuberous sclerosis complex (cannabidiol elevates mechanistic target of rapamycin inhibitor levels) and in a phase 1 healthy volunteer trial of coadministered everolimus and CBD.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Anti-aging drugs extend healthspan and are most effective before overt diseases cause organ damage and loss of function, so rapamycin is most effective when administered at the pre-disease or even pre-pre-disease stages of age-related diseases. It delays the onset of age-related diseases, which are manifestations of aging, and although rapamycin may reverse some manifestations of aging, it is more effective at slowing aging than reversing it. Rapalogs may slow atherosclerosis, preventing myocardial infarction, but are unlikely to help reverse an infarction, and rapamycin may be useful for osteoporosis though not for a broken hip after an osteoporotic fracture.

subject: Rapamycin
context: Excessive activation of the mTORC1 pathway leads to impaired proliferation and differentiation of stem cells, promoting their aging and apoptosis. Rapamycin's inhibition of mTORC1 can restore stem cell functionality and improve tissue regeneration, as demonstrated in animal models where it increased myogenic and chondrogenic differentiation of muscle cells and improved mesenchymal cell function in Klotho-deficient mice. The mechanism is mainly associated with activation of autophagy, which cleanses cells of damaged structures and increases their survival and resistance to stress, and rapamycin also induces growth factors such as IGF1 and VEGF.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin has been shown to prevent cognitive decline in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. The beneficial effects include reducing beta-amyloid deposition, reducing the phosphorylation of pathogenic tau, restoring blood flow in the brain, preserving the integrity of the blood-brain barrier, preventing neuronal loss, and improving cognitive function. In the nervous system more generally, rapamycin reduces oxidative stress, apoptosis, and accumulation of toxic protein aggregates such as amyloid-beta and phosphorylated tau, supporting its potential neuroprotective role in the context of neurodegeneration.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Rapamycin is the most effective known cancer-preventive agent in mice, extending the lifespan of cancer-prone mice, and it prevents lymphoma and some types of cancer in transplant patients. Although it was once feared that rapamycin might increase cancer risk, rapamycin analogs everolimus and temsirolimus are now widely used in cancer therapy. While carcinogens from tobacco cause lung cancer in mice, rapamycin decreases tobacco-induced lung cancer multiplicity by 90%, and rapamycin and everolimus are more effective for preventing cancer than treating it, with no study showing that mTOR inhibitors cause cancer.

subject: Rapamycin
context: In transgenic models predisposed to Alzheimer's disease-like pathology, rapamycin prevented memory deficits and reduced cognitive decline, and inhibition of mTOR by rapamycin abolished cognitive deficits and reduced amyloid-beta levels in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. These robust neurological effects contrast with a systematic review finding that rapamycin and its derivatives improved immune, cardiovascular, and integumentary systems in humans but not neurological systems.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: A prospective, randomized exploratory study by Chung et al. (2019) provided the first evidence that topical application of rapamycin can reduce cellular markers of aging in human skin. It showed a reduction in the senescent cell marker p16INK4A protein and improvement in the structural and functional parameters of skin by increasing collagen VII levels, with improvement in clinical and histological appearance. Additionally, rapamycin limits the translation of pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype factors such as IL-1, NF-kappaB, and STAT3, reducing the risk of cancer development in late life.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Aging is associated with weakened immunity and chronic inflammation, and the mTOR pathway plays a key role in these processes. Rapamycin reduces lymphocyte overactivation and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-4 and TNFalpha while increasing the number of regulatory T cells. Inhibition of mTORC1 reduces chronic inflammation by decreasing the activity of the NF-kappaB pathway and the NLRP3 inflammasome complex, resulting in reduced production of IL-1beta and IL-18 cytokines and reduced leukocyte infiltration. The immune effect is dose-dependent: lower doses are immunostimulatory while higher doses lead to immunosuppression.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Inhibition of the mTOR pathway and activation of autophagy lead to improved cellular homeostasis, reduced oxidative stress, and a slowing of aging processes across multiple model organisms. In the nervous system, rapamycin reduces oxidative stress, apoptosis, and the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates such as amyloid-beta and phosphorylated tau. By activating ATF4 and producing hydrogen sulfide, rapamycin increases the resistance of cells to oxidative stress, and in cardiac tissue it stimulates breakdown of damaged cytoplasmic elements, reduces oxidative stress, and supports tissue regeneration.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: The results of the PEARL study, a trial of low-dose intermittent rapamycin given for 48 weeks to adults aged 50-85, appear to confirm the possibility of pharmacological modulation of age-related inconveniences. Significant improvements in lean body mass, reduction of pain symptoms in women, and improvements in self-assessment of health and emotional well-being in both sexes were observed. Sarcopenia, defined as progressive loss of muscle mass and strength leading to physical deterioration and increased fall risk, is one of the key conditions targeted, and an ongoing randomized placebo-controlled study is testing intermittent sirolimus at 6 mg/week combined with a training program for sarcopenia prevention in the elderly.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: In tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), where mTOR pathway hyperactivation is a hallmark due to variants in TSC1 or TSC2, rapamycin prevents seizures, reduces mortality, and rescues neuropathology including glial proliferation and disrupted cortical architecture in mouse models. In the EXIST-3 phase III trial, adjunctive everolimus significantly reduced seizure frequency in treatment-resistant epilepsy due to TSC, with about 40% of high-dose patients achieving at least 50% seizure reduction versus 15% placebo, leading to regulatory approval.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: In clinical settings, rapamycin's immunosuppressive mechanisms increase infection risk and impair wound healing, especially in otherwise healthy individuals without clinical manifestations that outweigh the risk of side effects. Some early clinical studies suggest short-term rapamycin or rapalogs may improve aspects of immune function in older adults, but these relied on serologic responses to influenza vaccination, a marker with limited predictive value for broader immunocompetence. Broader measures including T cell repertoire diversity, innate immune activity, and real-world infection resistance remain underexplored.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: Studies using the Apc Min/+ mouse model of familial adenoma polyposis showed that enteral administration of rapamycin (eRapa) effectively inhibits the development of intestinal tumors by inhibiting the mTORC1 pathway and limiting proliferation of epithelial cells in intestinal crypts. Treatment led to increased survival of the animals, and in some cases lifespan was equal to that of wild-type mice. Importantly, rapamycin also prevented the development of induced colorectal cancer, confirming its chemopreventive effect, and providing a foundation for clinical trials of eRapa in humans with APC mutations.
source_document: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md

subject: Rapamycin
context: The success of rapamycin in mTORopathy models stems from clearly defined molecular etiology and robust biomarkers: highly penetrant mutations driving mTOR hyperactivation render the pathway an actionable target. In TSC and GATOR1-related models such as Nprl3 knockout mice, rapamycin prevented seizures, reduced mortality, and rescued neuropathology, including when delivered in utero or postnatally. Everolimus is used as precision therapy in GATOR1-related epilepsies.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: Resting Metabolic Rate
context: Across and within individuals, resting metabolic rate (RMR) is most strongly predicted by fat free mass (FFM), which typically accounts for roughly 60-80 percent of the variance in RMR. Larger organs such as liver, brain, heart, and kidneys are metabolically expensive, so differences in lean mass drive most of the between-individual variation in RMR. Within a single individual, day-to-day variability of RMR is small, and the residual variability not explained by FFM includes fat mass, age, thyroid status, and ambient temperature. Because lean tissue is the primary metabolic driver, changes in muscle mass through training can modestly raise RMR.

subject: Resting Metabolic Rate
context: After a single session of aerobic exercise, resting metabolic rate remains elevated above baseline for a period of 24 to 48 hours in young individuals. Studies summarized by Speakman show that following moderate exercise, RMR increased by roughly 3-8 percent over the subsequent day, and residual effects could still be measured up to 48 hours post-exercise, in some cases lasting three days. The magnitude and duration of this elevation depend on exercise protocol and subject fitness, and it is thought to reflect recovery processes, elevated sympathetic tone, and increased substrate cycling in the post-exercise period.

subject: Resting Metabolic Rate
context: Resting metabolic rate (RMR) is the rate at which the body consumes energy while at rest, and it is the single largest component of total daily energy expenditure (TEE), typically accounting for about 60-70 percent of daily energy use. It is measured under standardized conditions of rest, thermal neutrality, and a fasting state. Because RMR dominates total daily energy expenditure, any change in RMR, such as the transient elevation caused by exercise, has a disproportionate impact on overall energy balance and, over time, on body weight regulation. The review by Speakman focuses on how exercise-induced alterations in RMR influence energy balance.

subject: Resting Metabolic Rate
context: Athletes in heavy training display elevated resting metabolic rates compared with untrained individuals, largely because their higher fat free mass increases the metabolic load of lean tissues. Speakman notes that RMR measured in endurance athletes can be elevated by about 5-10 percent beyond the prediction for their body composition alone, an effect attributed to increased protein turnover, elevated sympathetic tone, and continued recovery processes in muscle. However, the review stresses that the majority of the difference in total daily energy expenditure between athletes and non-athletes arises from the energy cost of training itself, not from chronic elevation of RMR.

subject: Resting Metabolic Rate
context: Resting metabolic rate is modulated by thyroid hormones, which set the metabolic tone of the body by regulating mitochondrial oxygen consumption and cellular sodium-potassium ATPase activity in most tissues. Speakman reviews that both hypothyroid and hyperthyroid states shift RMR substantially, and that within the normal range thyroid status contributes to inter-individual variability in resting metabolic rate. However, training-induced changes in RMR are generally not mediated by changes in thyroid hormone levels, and short-term exercise does not consistently alter circulating thyroid hormone concentrations, indicating that the post-exercise RMR elevation is driven by other factors.

subject: Ribosomal Protein S6
context: Phosphorylated ribosomal protein S6 (phospho-S6) is used as a surrogate marker of mTORC1 activation, having been applied to resected brain tissue specimens and experimental models for mTOR pathway hyperactivation in TSC and other mTORopathies. However, phospho-S6 has not proven a consistent clinical biomarker, making it difficult to determine how the extent of mTOR inhibition, rapamycin blood levels, and seizure reduction correlate. In many aging studies, surrogate biomarkers of mTORC1 inhibition are underreported or inconsistently applied, making it hard to confirm outcomes truly reflect effective mTOR inhibition - a key gap in the rapamycin longevity literature.
source_document: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md

subject: SASP
context: Cellular senescence is a key response to various cellular stresses characterized by a permanent cell cycle arrest and the secretion of a pro-inflammatory cocktail of factors known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Senescence serves protective roles in embryonic development, tumour suppression and tissue repair, but persistent SASP activation leads to chronic inflammation contributing to tissue dysfunction, ageing and a broad spectrum of age-related diseases including cancer. This dual nature makes SASP a focal point for understanding both the protective and detrimental effects of senescence.
source_document: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md

subject: SASP
context: Many SASP-associated genes are linked to super-enhancer-like regions that are particularly sensitive to changes in histone acetylation, and such loci probably require sustained acetyl-CoA availability to maintain high transcriptional output, rendering them especially vulnerable to interventions that limit acetyl-CoA supply. SLC25A1 inhibition reduces chromatin accessibility at these SASP loci both in vitro and in vivo, selectively suppressing inflammatory gene expression. This positions mitochondrial metabolism as an upstream determinant of chromatin accessibility in senescent cells, aligning with previous reports linking citrate metabolism to SASP regulation.
source_document: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md

subject: SASP
context: Senescent stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment secrete soluble SASP factors that confer therapeutic resistance on residual cancer cells, including WNT16B, amphiregulin (AREG) and epiregulin (EREG). Conditioned media from bleomycin-senescent PSC27 stroma elevated viability, migration and invasion of prostate cancer lines (PC3, DU145, M12, LNCaP) and shifted their survival curves against mitoxantrone. Apigenin treatment of the stromal cells diminished this SASP-conferred resistance almost to basal levels and increased cancer cell apoptosis (caspase-3/7 activity).

subject: SASP
context: ChIP-seq analysis of histone H3 acetylation at lysine 27 (H3K27ac) showed that loci gaining acetylation during senescence are markedly reduced following mitochondrial clearance, and these regions are enriched for inflammatory and interleukin signalling pathways central to the SASP. A 51-gene SASP signature induced during senescence is suppressed upon mitochondrial removal, with genes such as IL6 and CCL2 showing coordinated decreases in chromatin acetylation and mRNA expression. Multiple nodes of the mitochondrial citrate-acetyl-CoA axis converge to control H3K27ac at SASP loci, selectively modulating inflammatory gene expression without affecting the senescence-associated cell cycle arrest.
source_document: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md

subject: Senescent Cells
context: Targeting mitochondrial citrate metabolism suppresses inflammation across tissues and improves tissue function and healthspan during ageing without detectable changes in p16 or p21 expression, consistent with SASP modulation rather than senolytic clearance of senescent cells. In aged muscle, senescent-like nuclei defined by the CoreScence gene signature are present at similar abundance and distribution across conditions despite reduced SASP-associated transcription and chromatin accessibility at loci such as Ccl2 and Igfbp4. In the liver, the abundance of p16-positive and/or p21-positive cells remains unchanged while their nuclear histone acetylation is reduced by CTPI2 treatment.
source_document: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md

subject: Sex Steroid Ablation
context: Sex steroid ablation (SSA), accomplished surgically or with LHRH analogue administration, is a long-standing strategy for thymic rejuvenation. Mice castrated before puberty show delayed thymic atrophy; removal of sex steroids after puberty restores thymic architecture, increases thymic cellularity and enhances thymopoiesis in aged mice and humans. The number of early thymic progenitors, which decrease with age, is normalized after surgical castration. Thymic regeneration following castration is reversed in a dose-dependent manner by administration of testosterone or estrogen, indicating that sex steroids are primary drivers of thymic involution.

subject: SIRT1
context: Overexpression of the NAD-dependent deacetylase sir-2.1, the C. elegans homolog of SIRT1, extends lifespan in a manner that requires activation of the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt). This links sirtuin biology to mitohormesis: the NAD+/sirtuin pathway modulates longevity through activation of mitochondrial UPR and FOXO signaling. SIRT1 also regulates the activity of the coactivator PGC-1alpha by deacetylation, thereby influencing mitochondrial biogenesis and the antioxidant stress-resistance program, connecting energy sensing to mitohormetic adaptation.

subject: SIRT1
context: SIRT1, a nuclear sirtuin dependent on NAD+, regulates PGC-1α, FOXO and NRF1 transcriptional programs that govern mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defenses and stress adaptation. Reduced NAD+ availability during aging compromises SIRT1 and SIRT3 activity, weakening these resilience programs and contributing to mitochondrial dysfunction and stem cell exhaustion. Because NAD+ decline arises from reduced biosynthesis and increased degradation via CD38, PARP1 and SARM1, NAD+ repletion (e.g., with nicotinamide riboside or NMN) restores sirtuin-dependent signaling, enhances UPRmt, improves mitochondrial membrane potential, and delays stem cell senescence - central to the metabolic ax...
source_document: _document_ - Mitochondrial Drivers Stem Cell Aging Inflammaging Bautista 2026.md

subject: SIRT3
context: SIRT3, a mitochondrial sirtuin whose activity depends on NAD+, weakens antioxidant defenses and mitochondrial detoxification when NAD+ is depleted during aging. Reduced SIRT3 activity compromises the deacetylation of mitochondrial antioxidant and metabolic enzymes, leaving cells vulnerable to ROS-driven mitochondrial damage. Together with SIRT1, SIRT3 regulates PGC-1α, FOXO and NRF1 transcriptional programs that coordinate mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant responses. Because NAD+ decline lowers SIRT3 function, NAD+ repletion is a strategy to restore sirtuin-dependent mitochondrial resilience, delay stem cell senescence, and dampen the ROS-NF-κB-inflammaging axis.
source_document: _document_ - Mitochondrial Drivers Stem Cell Aging Inflammaging Bautista 2026.md

subject: sjTREC
context: Single joint T cell receptor excision circle (sjTREC) analysis is a molecular marker for active thymopoiesis. Using sjTREC, researchers reported a steady three-log decline in circulating naive T cells across an 80-year human lifespan, and a significant decrease of sjTREC per milligram of mouse thymus tissue with increasing age in BALB/c mice (6-90 weeks), demonstrating gradual decrease in thymopoiesis with age similar to humans. The sjTREC assay was also used to show that ghrelin administration to aged mice increases the number of recent thymic emigrants exported to the periphery. It is thus a quantitative readout of thymic output used across species.

subject: SK61_2
context: S6K1/2 (SK61_2), activated by mTORC1 phosphorylation, inactivates IRS1 by phosphorylating it, forming the negative feedback loop that is central to the incoherent bivalent motif underlying rapamycin hormesis. This feedback arm is the backward reaction from the inhibited target (mTORC1) toward the Input node (IRS1, controlled by S6K1/2), and its low Michaelis-Menten constant in the saturated regime strongly increases the probability of biphasic dose-responses. S6K1/2 also deactivates mTORC2, and a significant negative correlation exists between the inhibition of the IRS1-insulin complex and mTORC2 deactivation by the same enzyme S6K1.

subject: SLC25A1
context: In human tissues (muscle, heart, hippocampus and kidney; GTEx), expression of the mitochondrial citrate transporter gene SLC25A1 positively correlates with a mitochondrial-dependent SASP gene signature and with canonical senescence markers p16 and p21, whereas chronological age alone shows little or no association. This links mitochondrial citrate metabolism to senescence-associated inflammatory programmes across diverse human tissues. The finding supports SLC25A1 inhibition as a therapeutic target that modulates the inflammatory output of senescent cells through metabolic-epigenetic coupling rather than through senescent cell elimination.
source_document: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md

subject: SLC25A1
context: SLC25A1, the mitochondrial citrate carrier, exports citrate from the mitochondrial matrix to the cytosol, where it can be converted to acetyl-CoA. SLC25A1 expression is significantly increased at both mRNA and protein levels in multiple senescence contexts, and this citrate export sustains the nucleocytosolic acetyl-CoA pool required for histone acetylation. Genetic ablation of SLC25A1 does not alter CDK inhibitor expression or cell cycle arrest but markedly reduces SASP gene expression, and inhibition with the third-generation inhibitor CTPI2 selectively suppresses SASP-associated inflammation without clearing senescent cells.
source_document: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md

subject: SOCS3
context: IDO1 is controlled post-translationally: phosphorylation of its ITIM motifs recruits SOCS3, leading to ubiquitination and degradation of IDO1 as a negative feedback mechanism. This degradation pathway limits IDO1 activity and terminates its immunosuppressive effects, representing a key regulatory checkpoint. IDO1 can also mediate non-enzymatic signaling such as PI3K activation. IDO2 may compete for heme and act as a negative regulator in some settings. These regulatory layers are important for therapeutic targeting of IDO1, as they influence the durability and magnitude of tryptophan depletion and kynurenine production in the tumor microenvironment.

subject: Solid Dispersion
context: Solid dispersions of fisetin are prepared by dispersing the drug in a hydrophilic polymer matrix such as polyvinylpyrrolidone or hydroxypropyl methylcellulose, converting crystalline fisetin into an amorphous form that dissolves much faster. The review describes how fisetin solid dispersions markedly increase the dissolution rate and apparent solubility relative to the free drug, leading to improved oral absorption and higher plasma concentrations in pharmacokinetic studies. Because dissolution is the limiting step in fisetin absorption, solid dispersion technology is one of the most straightforward and widely explored macro- to micro-scale strategies for improving its bioavailability.
source_document: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md

subject: Sulforaphane
context: Sulforaphane, found abundantly in broccoli sprouts, is highlighted as a potent activator of NRF2 and an upregulator of Phase II detoxification enzymes. NRF2 is one of the key stress-response pathways activated by the acute ROS pulse that defines mitohormesis, alongside AMPK, PGC-1alpha, and SIRT1. Cruciferous vegetables are therefore recommended in the dietary protocol as polyphenol-rich xenohormetins and NRF2 activators that support the hormetic response.

subject: Sympathetic Nervous System
context: The sympathetic nervous system is the fight, flight, or freeze branch of the autonomic nervous system. It releases adrenaline and cortisol to prepare the body for action during events such as a HIIT workout, cold plunge, or fasting. When the SNS is active, it forces the heart to beat faster and more rhythmically, thereby lowering HRV. Chronic sympathetic dominance keeps the system stuck in the on position, producing a chronically depressed HRV that signals under-recovery and overtraining rather than adaptation.

subject: TAK1
context: TAK1, a key cytoplasmic kinase in modulation of the SASP, is rapidly phosphorylated upon genotoxic stress and functionally participates in the transition of the acute stress-associated phenotype (ASAP) towards the SASP through dual feedforward mechanisms. Phosphorylation and activation of p38 MAPK occurs downstream of TAK1, followed by engagement of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway that supports the chronic secretory phenotype. Apigenin does not block ATM or TAK1 phosphorylation but abrogates the sequential molecular events downstream, acting through the HSPA8 hub to dampen p38 MAPK and downstream PI3K/Akt/mTOR engagement.

subject: TFEB
context: TFEB binds Rag GTPases as part of the amino acid-sensing machinery at the lysosomal surface, and this interaction is modulated by post-translational modification: oxidation of cysteine 212 inhibits TFEB's binding to Rag GTPases (PMID 31826695). The Rag GTPase complex is central to nutrient sensing, recruiting mTORC1 and its substrate machinery to the lysosome when amino acids are abundant, and TFEB's association with this complex links TFEB localization to nutrient availability. Oxidation at C212, by disrupting this binding, represents a redox-responsive mechanism that influences TFEB's cellular localization and activity, coupling oxidative stress to the regulation of the autophagy-lysosome pathway.

subject: TFEB
context: The acetyltransferase ACAT1 acetylates TFEB at multiple lysine residues with opposing functional outcomes: acetylation at K116 hinders TFEB binding to DNA (PMID 30059277), while acetylation at K91, K103, and K430 promotes nuclear translocation and DNA binding. These site-specific acetylation events modulate TFEB's ability to interact with chromatin and activate transcription of lysosomal and autophagic genes. The K116 acetylation that inhibits DNA binding is reversed by SIRT1 deacetylation, which enhances TFEB transcriptional activity. Together these marks show that acetylation acts as a dynamic post-translational switch controlling TFEB's DNA-binding capacity and thus its gene-regulatory output.

subject: TFEB
context: The acetyltransferase GCN5 acetylates TFEB at lysines K274 and K279, hindering TFEB binding to DNA and thus dampening its transcriptional output (PMID 31750630). Acetylation of these residues reduces TFEB's affinity for its target gene promoters, suppressing the expression of lysosomal and autophagic genes. This represents a second acetylation-based regulatory mechanism, complementary to ACAT1-mediated acetylation, by which TFEB's DNA-binding capacity is negatively controlled. Such marks illustrate the breadth of post-translational control over TFEB, where phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, SUMOylation, and other modifications converge to regulate the master regulator of cellular clearance.

subject: TFEB
context: The deacetylase SIRT1 deacetylates TFEB at lysine 116, and this deacetylation enhances TFEB transcriptional activity (PMID 27209302). SIRT1 reverses the inhibitory acetylation of K116 deposited by ACAT1, which hinders TFEB binding to DNA, thereby restoring TFEB's capacity to activate its target genes for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. This places TFEB under the control of the NAD+-dependent sirtuin SIRT1, linking cellular energy and redox status to the activity of the master transcriptional regulator of cellular clearance. The SIRT1/ACAT1 balance at K116 is a prototypical example of how a single residue integrates opposing enzymatic activities.

subject: TFEB
context: Calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB at S211 and S142, promoting nuclear translocation of the transcription factor (PMID 26043755). This dephosphorylation reverses the cytoplasmic-retention effect imposed by mTORC1 (S211) and ERK2/mTORC1 (S142) phosphorylation, allowing TFEB to enter the nucleus and activate lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy genes. Calcineurin is a calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase, so this pathway couples calcium signaling to the TFEB-mediated cellular clearance program. It forms the dephosphorylation arm of TFEB regulation alongside PP2A, providing a calcium-sensitive route to activate the autophagy-lysosome pathway under stress conditions.

subject: TFEB
context: The protein phosphatase PP2A dephosphorylates TFEB at S122 and at the cluster S109 and S114, promoting translocation of the transcription factor to the nucleus (PMID 29945972). Dephosphorylation of these sites reverses the cytoplasmic-retention effect of mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation at S122, releasing TFEB to enter the nucleus and activate lysosomal and autophagic gene transcription. This places protein phosphatase 2A as a counteracting force to nutrient-sensing kinase pathways, helping determine the net phosphorylation state of TFEB and thus its subcellular localization. Together with calcineurin, PP2A provides the dephosphorylation arm of TFEB's regulatory cycle.

subject: TFEB
context: Akt phosphorylates TFEB at serine 467, resulting in cytoplasmic retention of the transcription factor (PMID 28165011). This places TFEB downstream of PI3K/Akt signaling, so growth factor and insulin signals can restrain TFEB's nuclear translocation and thus suppress the lysosomal/autophagic transcriptional program. The S467 site is shared with AMPK, which phosphorylates the same residue to produce the opposite outcome - enhanced transcriptional activity - illustrating how different kinases can converge on a single phosphorylation site to generate context-dependent regulation of TFEB. Akt-mediated cytoplasmic retention keeps TFEB inactive in the cytosol until activating signals relieve the phosphorylation.

subject: TFEB
context: AMPK phosphorylates TFEB at serines 467, 466, and 469, and these phosphorylation events enhance TFEB's transcriptional activity (PMID 33734022). This is consistent with AMPK's role as an energy-stress sensor that promotes catabolic programs: when cellular energy is low, AMPK activates TFEB to drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. The S467 site is notable because Akt phosphorylates the same residue with the opposite effect (cytoplasmic retention), demonstrating that distinct upstream signals can use a single phosphorylation site to either activate or repress TFEB depending on context. AMPK phosphorylation thus couples cellular energy status to the autophagy-lysosome gene expression program.

subject: TFEB
context: ERK2 phosphorylates TFEB at serine 142, producing cytoplasmic retention and nuclear export of the transcription factor (PMID 21617040, 29992949). Phosphorylation at this site, shared with mTORC1 and CDK4/CDK6, keeps TFEB out of the nucleus and thereby represses its transcriptional program for lysosomal and autophagic genes. This places TFEB under the control of mitogen/extracellular-signal-regulated kinase (ERK) signaling in addition to nutrient sensing, integrating growth factor cues into the control of lysosome biogenesis and autophagy. Dephosphorylation of S142 by calcineurin reverses this effect and promotes TFEB translocation to the nucleus.

subject: TFEB
context: GSK3beta phosphorylates TFEB at serine 138, promoting lysosomal localization and nuclear export (PMID 27617930, 29992949), and at S134 promoting lysosomal localization. Phosphorylation of TFEB by GSK3beta modulates its subcellular distribution, controlling access of the transcription factor to its nuclear targets. The S138 site is particularly notable because it is also subject to O-GlcNAc glucosylation that blocks TFEB nuclear export, illustrating cross-talk between phosphorylation and glycosylation at the same residue. GSK3beta regulation of TFEB links glycogen synthase kinase signaling to the control of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy.

subject: TFEB
context: mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB at multiple sites with distinct functional consequences: phosphorylation at S211 and S122 causes cytoplasmic retention, at S142 it drives cytoplasmic retention and nuclear export, and at S138 it promotes nuclear export. Phosphorylation of these sites prevents TFEB from translocating to the nucleus, thereby limiting its transcriptional program. This is the canonical nutrient-sensing mechanism by which mTORC1 couples lysosomal and autophagic gene expression to amino acid availability. Dephosphorylation of S211 (by calcineurin) and S122 (by PP2A) releases this brake and allows TFEB nuclear translocation. Cited references include PMID 28055300 and 30120233.

subject: TFEB
context: The stress kinase p38 MAPK phosphorylates TFEB with context-dependent outcomes: phosphorylation at S211 causes cytoplasmic retention (PMID 34930303), while phosphorylation at S401 promotes nuclear translocation (PMID 36507874). The S211 site is the same residue phosphorylated by mTORC1, so p38 MAPK participates in the nutrient-independent control of TFEB localization, and phosphorylation at S401 conversely drives the transcription factor into the nucleus. This places TFEB downstream of cellular stress signaling via p38 MAPK, allowing stressors to modulate the lysosomal/autophagic transcriptional program. The opposing effects at different sites illustrate how site-specific phosphorylation integrates multiple signals into a final TFEB localization decision.

subject: TFEB
context: Protein kinase C beta (PKCbeta) phosphorylates TFEB at S466 and the cluster S461/S462 and S468, promoting its stability (PMID 23599343). Phosphorylation at S466 is shared with AMPK, which phosphorylates the same site to enhance transcriptional activity, while PKCbeta-mediated phosphorylation stabilizes the TFEB protein. By stabilizing TFEB, PKCbeta signaling can raise the cellular pool of the transcription factor available for nuclear translocation when other activating signals arrive. This illustrates how post-translational phosphorylation by multiple kinases converges on TFEB to control its abundance, localization, and activity, integrating diverse cellular signaling inputs into the regulation of lysosomal and autophagic gene expression.

subject: TFEB
context: TFEB is retained in the cytosol when it is phosphorylated at cytoplasmic-retention sites. Phosphorylation of S211 by mTORC1 or p38 MAPK, of S142 by mTORC1 or ERK2, of S122 by mTORC1, of S467 by Akt, and of S3 by MAP4K3 all promote cytoplasmic retention of TFEB, keeping the transcription factor away from its nuclear target genes. This phosphorylation-dependent cytosolic sequestration is the primary mechanism by which nutrient-rich and growth-factor-rich conditions suppress the lysosomal and autophagic transcriptional program. Dephosphorylation of these sites by calcineurin or PP2A relieves the retention and permits TFEB to translocate to the nucleus.

subject: TFEB
context: The E3 ubiquitin ligase STUB1 ubiquitinates TFEB, and this ubiquitination enhances TFEB activity (PMID 28754656). Rather than simply marking TFEB for degradation, ubiquitination by STUB1 in this case increases the transcription factor's functional output, consistent with the growing appreciation that ubiquitination can serve non-proteolytic regulatory functions. This adds TFEB to the set of proteins whose activity is tuned by ubiquitin conjugation. The finding illustrates the diversity of post-translational modifications - including ubiquitination, PARsylation, and SUMOylation in addition to phosphorylation and acetylation - that regulate TFEB's localization, stability, and transcriptional activity in the control of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy.

subject: TFEB
context: TFEB translocates to the nucleus in response to dephosphorylation of its cytoplasmic-retention sites. Dephosphorylation of S211 and S142 by calcineurin, and of S122 and S109/S114 by PP2A, promotes nuclear translocation, while phosphorylation of S401 by p38 MAPK also drives the transcription factor into the nucleus. Acetylation at K91/K103/K430 and PARsylation by TNKS1 likewise promote nuclear translocation, and O-GlcNAc glucosylation of S195/S196/S203/T201/T208 promotes nuclear entry while S138 glucosylation blocks nuclear export. Once in the nucleus, TFEB activates transcription of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy genes, making nuclear localization the key regulatory decision point.

subject: Thymic Epithelial Cells
context: Thymic epithelial cells produce a number of colony stimulating factors and hematopoietic cytokines, including IL-1, IL-3, IL-6, IL-7, TGF-β, oncostatin M, and leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF). Intrathymic and systemic production of these cytokines and growth factors regulates the complex process of thymopoiesis and is responsible for stromal cross-talk within the thymic microenvironment. IL-7 in particular is a crucial cytokine for thymocyte survival and T cell development, making the thymic cytokine milieu a candidate target for therapies aimed at reversing age-induced thymic involution. Loss of TEC-derived IL-7 production with age contributes to declining thymic output.

subject: Thymic Epithelial Cells
context: Thymic epithelial cells (TECs) in the cortex and medulla form a complex network that supports T cell differentiation, providing the essential microenvironment for productive thymopoiesis. The thymus consists of cells of stromal and hematopoietic origin, including TECs, mesenchymal cells (fibroblasts), endothelial cells and dendritic cells. Differentiating thymocytes migrate from the cortico-medullary junction through the cortex and back to the medulla, encountering functionally distinct microenvironments that regulate positive and negative selection.

subject: Thymic Involution
context: Age-associated thymic involution results in diminished thymopoiesis: reduction of the thymic epithelial space causes loss of T cell receptor gene rearrangement and decreased output of naive T cells to the periphery. Using single joint T cell receptor excision circle analysis (sjTREC), a molecular marker for active thymopoiesis, researchers measured a steady three-log decline in circulating naive T cells across an 80-year human lifespan. Similar decreases in sjTREC per milligram of thymus tissue were observed in aging BALB/c mice from 6 to 90 weeks. Thus involution reduces both the quantity and quality of T cells exported across the lifespan.

subject: Thymopoiesis
context: Thymopoiesis is the process by which T cell development, maturation and induction of self-tolerance occur in the thymic epithelial space. Lymphoid progenitors enter the thymus at the cortico-medullary junction, migrate to the outer cortex for early development and TCR gene rearrangement and positive selection, then return to the medulla for negative selection before export to the periphery. Reduction of functional thymopoiesis with aging results in loss of TCR gene rearrangement and decreased output of naive T cells to the periphery.

subject: Thymus
context: The thymus is a vital organ for homeostatic maintenance of the peripheral immune system. Within its two compartments, the true thymic epithelial space (TES, comprising cortex and medulla) and the perivascular space (PVS), T cells develop, mature, and undergo induction of self-tolerance in a process called thymopoiesis. The cortex hosts early thymocyte development including T cell receptor gene rearrangement and positive selection, while the medulla carries out negative selection to remove autoreactive T cells. The perivascular space, composed of adipocytes, peripheral lymphocytes and stroma, is a non-thymopoietic component.

subject: Thymus
context: The thymus exhibits profound age-associated involution, a striking paradoxical feature of this critical lymphoid tissue. Thymic function begins to decrease from the first year of life; the lymphoid component of the thymic epithelial space involutes roughly 3% per year through middle age (35-45 years) and about 1% per year thereafter, while the perivascular space expands with adipocytes and peripheral lymphocytes. By age 70, the TES falls below 10% of total thymus tissue. Although thymic decline is of minimal consequence to healthy individuals, the reduced efficacy of the aging immune system has direct etiological links with opportunistic infections, autoimmunity, and cancer burden.

subject: Toluidine Blue O
context: Toluidine blue O (TB), the 3,7-dimethyl analog of methylene blue, is the most potent of the tested phenothiazine derivatives, with EC50s of 1.75 nM for viability, 0.11 nM for ROS reduction, and 1.54 nM for preserving mitochondrial membrane potential in the HT-22 glutamate assay. Like MB, TB significantly increased the rate of cytochrome c reduction in the complex I-III assay with NADH as electron donor, enhanced cellular oxygen consumption, and decreased lactate production, sharing MB's alternative electron-transfer-carrier function but with greater potency.
source_document: _document_ - Neuroprotective Actions of Methylene Blue and Its Derivatives.md

subject: UCP3
context: Uncoupling protein 3 (UCP3) is expressed primarily in skeletal muscle and is a candidate mediator of the proton leak that contributes to resting metabolic rate and exercise-related energy expenditure. Speakman cites evidence that UCP3 mRNA is elevated after exercise and that its expression, together with UCP2, may account for a fraction of the exercise-induced rise in metabolic rate. The functional importance of UCP3 in mediating proton leak remains debated, because knockout studies in mice do not show gross changes in resting metabolic rate, but its induction by training and by lipids keeps it a focus for understanding inter-individual differences in energy expenditure.

subject: Urolithin A
context: Urolithin A is a mitophagy-enhancing intervention that selectively removes damaged mitochondria, improving muscle health in aged models. It represents one of the leading mitochondria-targeted anti-aging strategies, alongside NAD+ repletion (nicotinamide riboside, NMN), mitochondrial biogenesis activation (AMPK activators, PGC-1α pathway), mitochondrial transplantation (nMITO bioengineered mitochondria), mtDNA editing (mitoTALENs, mitoZFNs), and scalable mitochondrial transfer platforms.
source_document: _document_ - Mitochondrial Drivers Stem Cell Aging Inflammaging Bautista 2026.md

subject: Urolithin A
context: Urolithin A is a potent inducer of mitophagy, the clean-up process that recycles old, damaged mitochondria so new ones can take their place, and is described as a core mitohormetic mechanism. It is recommended to be taken with the first fat-containing meal of the day, as co-ingesting with healthy fats such as eggs, avocado, or yogurt can enhance its absorption. By supporting mitochondrial recycling, Urolithin A complements the energy production and renewal pathways targeted by the overall mitohormesis protocol.

subject: Valine
context: Valine metabolism involves conversion to succinyl-CoA, which enters the TCA cycle to produce ATP, making valine a gluconeogenic and anaplerotic amino acid. Restricting valine alone reduces body weight, improves metabolic health, reduces hepatic senescence, and extends lifespan of male mice, while in female mice valine restriction is protective in Alzheimer's disease progression. Dysregulated valine catabolism (via 3-hydroxyisobutyrate) contributes to insulin resistance in diabetic rats. Human plasma analysis found reduced circulating valine is associated with aging and moderate cognitive impairment, but valine supplementation worsens glucose tolerance and induces gut inflammation and hepatic lipid deposition, suggesting the role of valine in healthy aging may vary between species.

subject: Vitamin C
context: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) exhibits reducing properties similar to methylene blue and can serve as an alternative treatment for methemoglobinemia, though with significant limitations. Ascorbic acid reduces methemoglobin through a slower, nonenzymatic pathway that often requires multiple doses over several hours to achieve a significant effect. Although case reports demonstrate successful treatment with high-dose vitamin C, it is unlikely to be effective in a resuscitation situation. Vitamin C is most appropriate when methylene blue is contraindicated, such as in patients with G6PD deficiency, or when methylene blue is unavailable.

subject: Xenohormesis
context: Xenohormesis is the hypothesis that naturally occurring plant compounds - often synthesized when plants are under environmental stress such as drought - act as cross-species signaling molecules that induce a hormetic response when consumed by animals. These compounds are proposed to prepare the recipient organism for presumed worsening environmental conditions (famine for the animal, drought for the plant). This concept extends the hormesis framework to dietary phytochemicals and may help explain the medicinal value of certain plant-derived molecules.

subject: Zone 2 Cardio
context: Zone 2 cardio performed 3 to 4 times per week for 45-60 minutes builds the aerobic base, increases mitochondrial volume, and improves fat oxidation efficiency, and is the recommended low-intensity alternative when HRV is significantly below baseline and heavy stressors must be skipped. It is positioned as the aerobic foundation of the training protocol, complementing HIIT and sprint interval training done 1-2 times per week that generate the acute ROS spike and lactate accumulation to trigger PGC-1alpha, the master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis.
